tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. tools.name: mcp__8dd1f51a-ea67-45bd-9826-32d43cc850bd__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Apify

Apify is the world's largest marketplace of tools for web scraping, data extraction, and web automation.
These tools are called **Actors**. They enable you to extract structured data from social media, e-commerce, search engines, maps, travel sites, and many other sources.

## Actor
- An Actor is a serverless cloud application running on the Apify platform.
- Use the Actor's **README** to understand its capabilities.
- Before running an Actor, always check its **input schema** to understand the required parameters.

## Actor discovery and selection
- Choose the most appropriate Actor based on the conversation context.
- Search the Apify Store first; a relevant Actor likely already exists.
- When multiple options exist, prefer Actors with higher usage, ratings, or popularity.
- Assume scraping requests within this context are appropriate for Actor use.
- Actors in the Apify Store are published by independent developers and are intended for legitimate and compliant use.

## Actor execution workflow
- Actors take input and produce output.
- Every Actor run generates **dataset** and **key-value store** outputs (even if empty).
- Actor execution may take time, and outputs can be large.
- Large datasets can be paginated to retrieve results efficiently.

## Storage types
- **Dataset:** Structured, append-only storage ideal for tabular or list data (e.g., scraped items).
- **Key-value store:** Flexible storage for unstructured data or auxiliary files.

## Apify API resources
- Any Apify API GET endpoint can be read as an MCP resource. Pass the full `https://api.apify.com/v2/...` URL to `resources/read`; the server injects the session's Apify token and returns the response body. Reads require an Apify token — a session without one (e.g. payment-only x402/Skyfire) fails with a JSON-RPC error.
- Actor and tool results return storage IDs, not resource URLs — build the URL from the ID (e.g. a `datasetId` becomes `https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/{datasetId}/items`) and read it via `resources/read`.
- Reads inline up to ~256… [truncated]

## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

Retrieve only needed pages; do not re-scrape results that already contain the required content."],"success":true,"data":{"web":[{"url":"https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system","title":"How we built our multi-agent research system - Anthropic","description":"# How we built our multi-agent research system
We share the engineering challenges and the lessons we learned from building this system.

The journey of this multi-agent system from prototype to production taught us critical lessons about system architecture, tool design, and prompt engineering.

### Benefits of a multi-agent system
We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval.

### Architecture overview for Research
Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.

It then creates specialized Subagents (two are shown here, but it can be any number) with specific research tasks.

### Prompt engineering and evaluations for research agents
2. **Teach the orchestrator how to delegate.** In our system, the lead agent decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. We started by allowing the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage,' but found these instructions often were vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed the exact same searches as other agents. Workers never talk to each other.

# Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? The Research, the Case Studies, and the Fixes
AS

AgentSwarms Authors

July 9, 2026· 20 min read·619

Share

Multi-Agent SystemsFailure ModesReliability

One agent struggling with a hard task obviously becomes several agents that divide it up, check each other's work, and deliver something better. It is intuitive, it demos beautifully, and it is — according to a growing body of published evidence — frequently wrong. The uncomfortable finding is not that multi-agent systems are bad.

No invented statistics, no imagined incidents.

## Start with the uncomfortable finding
What came out is **MAST** — the Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy: **14 distinct failure modes** grouped into **three categories**. Crucially, they measured how often each one actually occurs.

MAST, from “Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?” — 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks. Percentages are the measured share of observed failures.

The MAST taxonomy with measured shares.

The single most common failure mode is **step repetition (17.14%)** — agents redoing work they have already done. Second is **reasoning-action mismatch (13.98%)** — an agent reasons its way to a correct conclusion and then does something else. Third is **failing to ask for clarification (11.65%)**. Meanwhile the failure everyone worries about — one agent ignoring another's input — accounts for **0.17%**.

The failures are organizational, not intellectual

Almost none of the top failure modes are “the model wasn't smart enough.” They are agents repeating themselves, not stopping, not asking, not checking, and doing something other than what they just reasoned. These are the failures of a badly-run team, not a stupid one.

## Three case studies from people who actually shipped
Academic taxonomies are only half the picture. Tap between all three:

On their ProgramDev benchmark, ChatDev scored just 33.33% correctness.

The numbers are each organization's own, not ours — links in the references.

## The deeper reason: compounding, not stupidity
Underneath every failure mode in MAST sits a piece of arithmetic that no amount of model progress erases.

Per-step reliability95%Sequential agent steps10

59.9%

95% ^ 10 = 59.9%

A 95%-reliable agent run 20 times in sequence completes the whole chain correctly only about 36% of the time.

This is why the MAST failure modes cluster where they do. **Step repetition** and **unaware of termination conditions** are what a system does when nothing tells it to stop. **Premature termination** and **no or incomplete verification** are what happens when nothing checks whether the chain actually succeeded.

## How to prevent it
The good news about a taxonomy with measured frequencies is that it tells you exactly where to spend your effort.

Every unchecked box corresponds to a failure mode that was actually measured in the MAST traces.

- **Write the spec down, per agent** — an explicit role, an explicit tool allowlist, and an explicit stop condition. “Unaware of termination conditions” is 9.82% of failures on its own.

Getting Up to Speed on MAS

## MAST: 14 Failure Modes from 1,600 Traces
**Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?** **(MAST)** [arXiv 2503.13657](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657) · NeurIPS 2025 D&B

1,600 annotated traces across 7 frameworks. First empirical taxonomy of why MAS break.

Core contribution: MAST taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 categories

- 1,600+ traces across MetaGPT, ChatDev, HyperAgent, AppWorld, AG2, Magentic-One, OpenManus
- 41 to 87 percent failure rates across all frameworks; systemic, not isolated
- Top 3 failures: step repetition (15.7 percent), reasoning-action mismatch (13.2 percent), unaware of termination (12.4 percent)
- Systems with explicit verifiers (MetaGPT, ChatDev) had fewer failures
- Inter-agent failures require "theory of mind"; agents can't model each other's information needs
- Adding high-level objective verification gave +15.6 percent improvement
- LLM-as-Judge pipeline: 94 percent accuracy against human experts

Cemri, Pan, Yang, Agrawal, Chopra, Tiwari, Keutzer, Parameswaran, Klein, Ramchandran, Zaharia, Gonzalez, Stoica

The MAST paper is the one I keep coming back to. It’s the first rigorous empirical study of multi-agent failures. The authors took 1,600 execution traces from seven popular multi-agent frameworks, annotated each one with human experts, and built a 14-mode failure taxonomy.

The headline number is that every framework they tested had failure rates between 41 and 87 percent. Every single one. These are the production frameworks. These are the systems people cite in their papers. And they fail almost as often as they succeed.

#### MAST's 14 Failure Modes
FC1 System Design

Disobey task spec (11.8%)Disobey role spec (1.5%)Step repetition (15.7%)Loss of conversation history (2.8%)Unaware of termination (12.4%)

FC2 Inter-Agent

Conversation reset (2.2%)Fail to ask for clarification (6.8%)Task derailment (7.4%)Information withholding (0.85%)Ignored other agent's input (1.9%)Reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%)

FC3 Verification

Premature termination (6.2%)No/incomplete verification (8.2%)Incorrect verification (9.1%)

The taxonomy matters because it lets you diagnose specific failures. When someone says “my agent got stuck in a loop,” you can now ask whether that’s step repetition (FM-1.3) or conversation reset (FM-2.1). Those have different causes and different fixes.

The finding that the paper downplays but I think is most important: the inter-agent failures are the hardest to fix. FC1 issues are prompt engineering problems. You can get meaningful improvements by rewriting role specifications. FC2 issues require what the paper calls “theory of mind,” meaning the agents don’t accurately model each other’s information needs. Prompt fixes don’t help there. The solutions are structural.

A [useful paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657) that captures a taxonomy of failure cases in agent systems, specifically where multiple agents are involved. | **Code** | **Failure Mode** | **Description** |

Many failures came from **system design, not just limitations of the underlying LLMs** (e.g., hallucination or basic prompt following).

**Paper:** "Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems" (arXiv:2512.08296)
**Authors:** Yubin Kim, Ken Gu, Chanwoo Park, and 16 other co-authors, including Xin Liu (19 authors total)
**Dates:** Submitted 9 December 2025 (v1); latest revision 8 April 2026 (v3)

**Key findings**

- **Scale of study:** 260 configurations across six agentic benchmarks, three LLM families, and five architectures: Single-Agent plus four multi-agent types (Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid). Tools, prompts, and compute were standardized.
- **Predictive model accuracy:** Cross-validated R² = 0.373 across all six benchmarks, rising to 0.413 with a task-grounded capability metric.
- **Capability saturation:** Coordination yields diminishing returns once single-agent baselines exceed a certain performance level. The page does not give the numeric threshold.
- **Tool-heavy tasks:** These appear to incur multi-agent overhead. No numeric trade-off is given.
- **Error propagation:** Architectures without centralized verification tend to propagate errors more than those with centralized coordination. No amplification factors are given for independent versus centralized designs.
- **Performance range vs. single-agent baseline:** From +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning (the most parallelizable task reported) to -70.0% on sequential planning.
- **Architecture selection:** The framework identifies the best-performing architecture for 87% of held-out configurations and shows consistent architecture preferences on unseen frontier models.
- **Core conclusion:** As the paper puts it, "architecture-task alignment determines collaborative success."

**Not available in the provided content:** The names of the six benchmarks, the numeric capability saturation threshold, error amplification factors, the numeric tool-coordination trade-off, and the full abstract text. **Authors:** Bochen Han and Songmao Zhang
**Submitted:** 2 July 2025 (v1 only, 1,399 KB)

**Abstract (paraphrased):** The authors propose adding a blackboard architecture to LLM multi-agent systems (MAS). Agents with different roles can see all shared information and other agents' messages throughout problem-solving. The agents that act are chosen based on the blackboard's current contents. This select-and-execute cycle repeats until the blackboard reaches a consensus. The paper presents the first implementation of this idea and tests it on commonsense, reasoning, and math datasets. The authors report that it is competitive with state-of-the-art static and dynamic MAS, achieves the best average performance, and uses fewer tokens. They suggest it could suit problems where no well-defined workflow exists.

I found LangChain's June 2025 post on benchmarking multi-agent architectures, but the search didn't return its actual score table, so I can't give you the numeric results.

**What the study did:** LangChain benchmarked a modified version of the τ-bench dataset. They added 6 additional environments to the dataset: home improvement, tech support, pharmacy, automotive, restaurant, and Spotify playlist management. The aim was to test how multi-agent systems handle more complicated domains. None of these synthetic domains are required (or useful) for the completion of any of the tasks in the original dataset.

**The architectures compared:**
- **Single agent:** A baseline in which one prompt has access to all tools and instructions. The Single Agent model serves as a baseline, utilizing a single prompt to access all tools and instructions.
- **Supervisor:** A central agent receives user input and delegates to sub-agents. The post notes only the supervisor agent can respond to the user. It was built with the langgraph-supervisor package and places very little assumptions on the sub agents.
- **Swarm:** Sub-agents hand control to one another. It was built with langgraph-swarm, but this requires each sub-agent knowing all other agents in the architecture.

**Key finding:** The post's headline claim is that LangChain made improvements to its "supervisor" implementation that yielded a nearly 50% increase in performance on this benchmark. The earlier single-agent study had found a significant decrease in performance with increased context-size, even if that context was irrelevant to the target task. That is the main motivation for splitting work across agents.

**Caveats:**
- The metrics are score and token cost. One version of the page has a placeholder where the scoring method should be named ("as measured by XYZ"), so the text is unfinished. Check the full post or the linked repo for the actual numbers.
- A separate academic study (MABench, derived from τ-bench) found that more complex architectures do not necessarily guarantee superior performance, and that the choice of optimal architecture strongly depends on the application domain and operational constraints.
- I found nothing about "translation" in the context of these benchmarks. If you meant the handoff mechanism, the swarm architecture is the one built around agent-to-agent handoffs.

**1. Architecture**
- Uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: a lead agent plans the work, spawns subagents to search in parallel, and synthesizes their findings.
- The lead saves its plan to Memory, because the context window is truncated beyond 200,000 tokens.
- Subagents run their own searches, use interleaved thinking to evaluate tool results, and return findings to the lead.
- The lead decides whether more research is needed, and can create more subagents or refine its strategy.
- Once research is done, a CitationAgent processes the documents and report to attribute claims to sources.
- Unlike static RAG, the system runs a multi-step search that adapts to new findings.

**2. Performance numbers**
- A multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead, Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) beat single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research eval.
- On BrowseComp, three factors explained 95% of performance variance. Token usage alone explained 80%, with tool calls and model choice as the other two.
- Agents use about 4× the tokens of chat interactions; multi-agent systems use about 15×.
- Parallelization cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries.
- Improving tool descriptions via a tool-testing agent reduced task completion time by 40%.
- Scaling guidance: simple fact-finding uses 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls; comparisons use 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each; complex research can use more than 10 subagents.

**3. Poor fits for multi-agent systems**
- Domains where all agents must share the same context.
- Tasks with many dependencies between agents.
- Most coding tasks, which have fewer parallelizable parts than research.
- Low-value tasks, since token costs may not be justified.
- Real-time coordination and delegation between agents, which LLM agents are not yet good at.

**4. Prompt engineering lessons**
- **Think like your agents:** simulate runs with the exact prompts and tools to find failure modes.
- **Teach delegation:** give each subagent an objective, output format, tool/source guidance, and task boundaries. Vague instructions led to duplicated work.
- **Scale effort to complexity:** embed explicit effort rules in prompts to prevent overinvestment in simple queries.
- **Tool heuristics:** examine all available tools first, match tool use to intent, prefer specialized tools over generic ones, and give each tool a distinct purpose and clear description.
- **Start wide, then narrow:** begin with short, broad queries, then progressively focus.
- **Parallel tool calling:** the lead spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel, and subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. Early sequential searches were "painfully slow."

**5. Synchronous execution and asynchronous challenges**
- The lead waits for each set of subagents to finish before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks.
- The lead cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the system can stall on one slow subagent.
- Asynchronous execution would add parallelism but introduces challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across subagents.

**6. Filesystem/artifact outputs**
- Subagents can store their outputs in external systems and pass lightweight references back to the coordinator.
- This reduces information loss in multi-stage processing and cuts the token overhead of copying large outputs through conversation history.
- It works especially well for structured outputs like code, reports, or data visualizations.

**7. Stateful errors and evaluation**
- Agents are stateful, so errors compound. Minor system failures can be catastrophic for long-running agents.
- Rather than restarting, the system resumes from where the agent was when the error occurred.
- Deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints are combined with the agent's ability to adapt, such as telling it when a tool is failing.
- For evaluation, focus on end-state outcomes rather than turn-by-turn steps, and break complex workflows into checkpoints.

**8. Lead agent steering while subagents run**
- The lead cannot steer subagents once they are running, because execution is synchronous.
- Subagents cannot coordinate with each other during execution.
- Steering is limited to the instructions given at spawn time; asynchronous execution is proposed as a future improvement.

## 1. Fleet-memory failure modes (§4)

- **Unauthorized leakage (§4.1):** "An agent retrieves memory outside its authorized scope." Example: a support agent retrieves billing notes meant only for finance agents.
- **Stale propagation (§4.2):** "Memory updates fail to synchronize correctly across agents." Example: one agent updates a shipping address while another still reads the old value.
- **Contradiction persistence (§4.3):** "Conflicting memories coexist without resolution." Example: two incompatible user preferences are both retrievable.
- **Provenance collapse (§4.4):** "Retrieved memories cannot be traced to their origin." The system can show that a fact is present, but not how it got there.

Conflicting writes are the contradiction case above. The paper does not define a separate "conflicting writes" category.

## 2. Proposed mechanisms

- **Scoped retrieval (§5.2, §5.5):** Four scopes (agent-local, team-shared, tenant-global, restricted). Policy is checked on every retrieval, not just semantic similarity.
- **Temporal resolution and supersession (§5.3):** "contradictory writes are resolved through temporal ordering and policy-aware resolution rules." Older rows are marked outdated or non-active (§8.4).
- **Conflict detection (§7.2, §8.4):** A structural detector uses RDF-triple compatibility on single-valued predicates. It runs post-commit and asynchronously.
- **Deduplication gate (§9.2):** A synchronous near-duplicate check rejects writes with HTTP 409 before the contradiction detector sees them.
- **Provenance tracking (§5.4):** Stores writer identity, source system, derivation history, and modification lineage. Derivation is recorded via `metadata.derived_from` (§7.3).
- **Policy-governed retrieval (§5.5):** Five steps: semantic candidate generation, policy filtering, temporal resolution, provenance enrichment, ranked delivery.
- **Propagation (§6.1, §9.3):** The `/memories/redistribute` endpoint re-homes a memory to another agent and requires trust level ≥3. The authors argue fleet-internal propagation should be available at a lower trust level.
- **Not covered:** The paper does not describe subscriptions, notifications, or push-based invalidation. Its propagation is measured by polling `/search`. Versioning appears only as supersession links and modification lineage.

## 3. Quantitative results

**Contradiction (§8.4, Table 2; N=200 fact-runs)**
- Detection rate, all fact-runs: 0.490 (98/200; 95% CI [0.422, 0.559]).
- Detection rate, both writes admitted: 1.000 (90/90; CI [0.959, 1.000]).

**Propagation (§8.3)**
- Fleet-sibling visibility: 117/120 (0.975; CI [0.929, 0.991]).
- Cross-fleet leak rate: 0/80.
- Write-to-visible window, strong mode (n=88): p50 0.83 s, max 1.97 s.

**Leakage (§8.1, §9.1)**
- Search leak rate across fleets: 0.439 (72/164). Search miss rate: 0.143 (4/28).

**Caveats (§10):** Self-evaluation by the authors, a single tenant, no baseline comparison, and cross-tenant probes not measured.

- **Identity and ownership (§6.1):** tenant ID, fleet ID, writing agent (`agent_id`), content.

## (1) How the blackboard mechanism works

- **Volunteering:** The abstract says subordinate agents "volunteer to respond based on their capabilities." §1 adds that "each agent retains full autonomy whether to participate in the task or not."
- **Decision logic:** File agents decide using their offline analysis of their partition (§3.2). The search agent first checks feasibility and refuses requests that need local files. The paper does not describe a confidence score or an explicit scoring step. The decision prompts are in Figures 5–7, which are not in the provided text.
- **Use of responses:** Collected responses become the observation for the requesting action. The main agent then decides whether to use or ignore them (§3). The main agent has at most T=10 actions (§4.1).

**ReWOO abstract claims (arXiv:2305.18323)**

- **Decoupling reasoning from observations:** ReWOO (Reasoning WithOut Observation) separates the reasoning process from external tool observations, rather than interleaving tool calls with reasoning as existing systems do.
- **Token efficiency:** The paper reports "5x token efficiency" on HotpotQA, a multi-step reasoning benchmark.
- **Accuracy:** It reports a "4% accuracy improvement" on HotpotQA.
- **Tool-failure robustness:** The abstract says ReWOO "demonstrates robustness under tool-failure scenarios."
- **Model offloading:** Decoupling enables instruction fine-tuning that moves reasoning from a 175B GPT-3.5 model into a 7B LLaMA model.
- **Planner/worker/solver:** This terminology does not appear in the page content, so I can't confirm it from this source.

**Authors:** Binfeng Xu, Zhiyuan Peng, Bowen Lei, Subhabrata Mukherjee, Yuchen Liu, and Dongkuan Xu

**Date:** Submitted 23 May 2023 (v1)

**Two orchestration approaches**

- **LLM-driven:** The LLM plans and decides its steps. The doc describes agents as "an LLM equipped with instructions, tools and handoffs." The LLM can autonomously plan, use tools, and delegate to sub-agents.
- **Code-driven:** Your code defines the agent flow. The doc says this approach "makes tasks more deterministic and predictable, in terms of speed, cost and performance."
- The two can be combined, and each has its own tradeoffs.

**Agents as tools vs. handoffs**

- **Agents as tools:** A manager agent keeps control of the conversation and calls specialists through `Agent.as_tool()`. Use this when one agent should own the final answer or combine outputs from several specialists.
- **Handoffs:** A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist, which becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. Use this when the specialist should respond directly.
- You can combine them: a triage agent hands off to a specialist, which can still call other agents as tools for narrow subtasks.

**LLM-orchestration best practices**

- Write clear prompts that specify available tools, how to use them, and constraints.
- Monitor the app and iterate on prompts based on failures.
- Let agents introspect and improve, such as by running in a loop or critiquing their own output.
- Use specialized agents rather than one general-purpose agent.
- Invest in evals to train and improve agents over time.

**Code-orchestration patterns**

- **Structured outputs:** Generate inspectable data, such as a category, and choose the next agent based on it.
- **Chaining:** Pass one agent's output as the next agent's input, e.g., research, outline, draft, critique, revise.
- **Evaluator loop:** In a `while` loop, run a task agent, then an evaluator agent that gives feedback, and stop when criteria are met.
- **Parallel execution:** Run independent agents concurrently with `asyncio.gather`. The doc notes this is "useful for speed when you have multiple tasks that don't depend on each other."

Examples are available in `examples/agent_patterns`.

**A2A agent cards and capability discovery**

- The Agent Card is the discovery manifest. Sources describe it as a JSON document at a well-known URI, with the v1.0 path at `/.well-known/agent-card.json` An A2A-speaking service hosts a JSON manifest at the well-known URI /.well-known/agent-card.json.

- Discovery is decentralized. One source says you don't register in a central directory, you just expose your card. Another notes that cards can also be found through registries or direct configuration.
- Clients use the card to decide how to act. A client can read the supported interfaces and skills, and check whether streaming or push notifications are available identifies the available skills, checks supported media types, and determines whether features such as streaming, push notifications, or an extended authenticated Agent Card are available.

**Routing queries to data sources (multi-source RAG, 2025)**

- Routing picks sources per query. One 2025 paper says routing also governs data source selection. It describes routers that map queries to the most relevant data sources and to orchestrate hybrid retrieval workflows.
- Standard multi-source RAG has a known weakness. One Cohere guide notes that the usual approach aggregates retrieved documents from all the different sources it is connected to, which may contribute to noise from less relevant documents.
- Lightweight classifiers can do the selection. RAGRoute, a 2025 federated search method, dynamically selects relevant data sources at query time using a lightweight neural network classifier.
- Source selection can be learned. Self-Routing RAG treats selective retrieval as knowledge source selection and treats the LLM itself as a first-class knowledge source.

**CrewAI Flows (`@start`, `@listen`, state)**

- **Entry points:** The `@start()` decorator marks where a Flow begins. You can declare several unconditional starts, gate one on a prior method or router label, or attach a callable condition. All satisfied @start() methods will execute (often in parallel) when the Flow begins or resumes.
- **Listeners:** The @listen() decorator is used to mark a method as a listener for the output of another task in the Flow. You can reference the upstream method by name as a string or pass the method object directly. The listener receives the upstream output as an argument.
- **State:** The docs' example uses a Pydantic model as the flow state, with `Flow[ExampleState]`. Each method reads and writes `self.state`, and the final state can be printed after `kickoff()`. CrewAI Flows provides robust mechanisms for both unstructured and structured state management, allowing developers to choose the approach that best fits their application's needs.
- **Output:** When you run a Flow, the final output is determined by the last method that completes.
- **Gap:** My search didn't return the `@router` section or the detailed state-persistence docs. I'd check the current Flows page for those. Also, the CrewAI docs are versioned (v1.10 through v1.15 pages appeared in results), so confirm the version you're using.

**LangGraph supervisor and swarm handoffs (`Command`)**

- **Command primitive:** The mechanic that makes all three patterns possible is the Command primitive. A node can return a `Command` that carries both a state update and the next node to run. The `goto` field names the destination, and `update` carries the state change. One example is a `Command` that targets a node in the parent graph, which helps with hierarchical setups.
- **Supervisor:** There is no add_edge from supervisor to anything — routing happens at runtime, from inside the function. The prebuilt `langgraph-supervisor` package wires this up via `create_supervisor`. Its default handoff tools pass the full message history to the sub-agent along with a tool message confirming the transfer. You can customize the tool name, description, and arguments, such as a task description for the next agent. However, the LangChain reference now recommends using the supervisor pattern directly via tools rather than this library for most use cases.
- **Swarm:** Each agent has handoff tools to its peers and decides itself when to pass control. The graph tracks an active_agent in state; whoever last handed off is who runs next time. The `langgraph-swarm` package provides `create_swarm` and `create_handoff_tool` for this pattern.
- **Handoff tools with `create_react_agent`:** The LangChain docs describe a special tool that returns a `Command` with `goto` set to the target agent and `update` set to the data to pass along. The docs say the navigation can target an agent node in a parent graph.

**Comparison:** A supervisor is a central router that gets control back after each step. A swarm has no central router, and agents hand off directly to peers. Both rely on `Command` (or handoff tools that return one).

Sources: the CrewAI docs pages, the LangChain multi-agent prebuilt docs, the `langgraph-supervisor` PyPI page and reference, and the LangChain blog post on Command. The Command blog post and the neurals.ca and wec.wiline.com write-ups are third-party, so check them against the official docs before relying on them.

## LbMAS: Key Details

**Components**
- **Control unit:** An LLM that selects which agents act each round. The paper says it "iteratively selects agents based on query q, current messages B on the blackboard and agent abilities."
- **Blackboard:** Has a public space and private spaces. The public space is shared by all agents. Private spaces are used "solely for those involved in a debate or verification of private matter."
- **Agent group:** Query-specific experts from an agent-generation module, plus predefined agents: decider, planner, critic, conflict-resolver, and cleaner.

**Predefined agent roles**
- **Planner:** Makes plans and decomposes complex queries into smaller tasks.
- **Critic:** Points out errors in blackboard messages, which may be LLM hallucinations, and forces relevant agents to rethink their output.
- **Decider:** Checks whether the blackboard holds enough information to give a final solution.
- **Conflict-resolver:** Detects contradictions and names the agents with conflicting messages. Those agents discuss, possibly in the private space, then each writes a new message to the public space.
- **Cleaner:** Detects useless or redundant messages and removes them to preserve quality and reduce tokens.

**Control unit selection**
Each round, the control unit chooses agents using the query, the current blackboard contents, and each agent's described abilities. The paper's ablation found that letting agents decide on their own, without the control unit, raised token cost sharply (e.g., 13.86M vs. 4.72M on MATH) with only slight performance changes.

**Termination**
- The decider gives a solution and the cycle stops, or
- the maximum of 4 rounds is reached.
- Then all agents answer, and the answer with the highest cumulative similarity to the others is chosen.
- Decider and majority-vote results were similar. Consensus rates were 89.8% (MMLU), 52.5% (GPQA), and 29.4% (MATH).

**Cleaner ablation**
Marking redundant messages instead of removing them lowered scores (e.g., MATH 71.00 vs. 72.60), which the paper cites as evidence for managing blackboard content.

**Benchmark results (Table 1, average)**
- LbMAS: 81.68
- Chateval: 80.56
- CoT (Qwen): 80.09
- Vanilla (Llama): 54.74

The paper reports average gains of 4.33% over CoT and 5.02% over static methods.

**Token comparison on MATH (Table 3, total tokens / score)**
- MultiPersona: 2,171,890 / 65.80
- LbMAS: 4,721,489 / 72.60
- Chateval: 5,451,820 / 70.20
- GPTSwarm: 5,449,425 / 67.25
- EoT: 8,328,772 / 60.40
- MaAS: 13,012,658 / 70.77
- AFlow: 16,697,032 / 69.25

The paper calls LbMAS's cost "the second lowest," but by these totals it is third lowest, behind MultiPersona. LbMAS has the highest score in this group, and the autonomous baselines spend extra tokens on a search step before solving.

**1. Five progress-ledger questions (each inner-loop step)**
- Is the request fully satisfied (task complete)?
- Is the team looping or repeating itself?
- Is forward progress being made?
- Which agent should speak next?
- What instruction or question should be asked of this team member?

**2. Task ledger contents**
- **Facts:** given or verified facts, plus facts to look up (e.g., via web search) and facts to derive (programmatically or by reasoning).
- **Educated guesses:** these let the Orchestrator express memorized knowledge in a qualified way. They are updated periodically by the outer loop.
- **Plan:** a step-by-step natural-language plan of steps and agent assignments. It is built only after the facts and guesses are populated. The plan is a hint, not a strict script: "neither the Orchestrator nor the other agents are required to follow it exactly."

**3. Stall counter and response**
- The Orchestrator increments a counter when it detects a loop or lack of forward progress.
- In the experiments, the threshold is ≤2. While the counter stays at or below it, the inner loop continues by selecting the next agent and instruction.
- Above the threshold, the Orchestrator exits the inner loop and runs a reflection and self-refinement step. It identifies what went wrong and what it learned, updates the task ledger, and revises the plan.
- Each plan update forces all agents to clear their contexts and reset their states.

**4. Benchmark results (test sets unless noted)**

| Benchmark | Magentic-One (GPT-4o) | Magentic-One (GPT-4o, o1) |
|---|---|---|
| GAIA | 32.33 ± 5.3 | 38.00 ± 5.5 |
| AssistantBench (exact match) | 11.0 ± 4.6 | 13.3 ± 4.9 |
| AssistantBench (accuracy) | 25.3 ± 6.3 | 27.7 ± 6.5 |
| WebArena (all 812 tasks) | 32.8 ± 3.2 | Not reported |

- WebArena validation split: 35.1% (148/422). Test split: 30.5% (119/390).
- Reference points: human GAIA 92.00; human WebArena 78.2.

**5. Ablations (GAIA validation, GPT-4o)**
- **Orchestrator:** replacing the ledger-based Orchestrator with a simple GroupChat-style one (no ledgers, planning, progress tracking, or loop detection) causes a drop of "31%" in performance.
- **Individual agents:** removing any single worker reduces performance by roughly 21% (Coder, Executor) to 39% (FileSurfer).
- **Level-specific effects:** FileSurfer is essential for Level 2, and WebSurfer is most essential for Level 1.
- The paper also notes that remaining agents sometimes compensated creatively for missing capabilities.

**6. Error analysis**
- **Most common:** persistent-inefficient-actions, where agents keep unproductive behavior without adapting after failures.
- **Second:** insufficient-verification-steps, where tasks are marked complete without adequate validation.
- **Third:** inefficient-navigation-attempts, which is especially prevalent in WebArena logs.
- **Also prevalent:** underutilized-resource-options, where agents fail to use available data, tools, or resources.
- The text does not give numeric counts for these codes; they appear only in Figure 4.

**7. Termination**
- The inner and outer loops end when the Orchestrator determines the task is complete, or when configurable termination logic is triggered, such as a maximum number of attempts or a maximum time limit.
- The paper cites a time budget of, for example, 25 minutes.
- At termination, the Orchestrator reviews the full transcript and ledger, then reports either a final answer or its best educated guess.

**Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)** induces reusable workflows, which the abstract describes as "commonly reused routines," from past experience. It then gives relevant workflows to the agent to guide later actions.

**When induction happens:**
- **Offline:** workflows are induced from training examples beforehand.
- **Online:** workflows are induced on the fly from test queries.

**Results:**
- **Mind2Web:** 24.6% relative improvement in success rate over baselines.
- **WebArena:** 51.1% relative improvement in success rate.
- **Steps:** AWM reduces the number of steps needed to successfully solve WebArena tasks.
- **Generalization:** Online AWM generalizes across tasks, websites, and domains. Its advantage over baselines grows from 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as the gap between training and test distributions widens.
- **Benchmarks:** The two benchmarks together cover 1,000+ tasks from 200+ domains, including travel, shopping, and social media.

**Metadata:** Authors are Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jiayuan Mao, Daniel Fried, and Graham Neubig. The paper (arXiv:2409.07429, cs.CL) was submitted on September 11, 2024.

**Paper:** "STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?" (arXiv:2605.06527, cs.CL)
**Authors:** Hanxiang Chao, Yihan Bai, Rui Sheng, Tianle Li, Yushi Sun
**Date:** Submitted 7 May 2026

**What STALE measures:** The ability of LLM agents to revise stored beliefs in long-term personalized memory when new evidence arrives. The authors argue that existing benchmarks mainly test static fact retrieval.

**Task types:** The benchmark has 400 expert-validated conflict scenarios, with 1,200 evaluation queries across three probing dimensions. The scenarios cover over 100 everyday topics, with contexts up to 150K tokens. The three dimensions are:
- **State Resolution:** detecting that a prior belief is outdated.
- **Premise Resistance:** rejecting queries that falsely presuppose a stale state.
- **Implicit Policy Adaptation:** proactively applying updated states in downstream behavior.

**Best model accuracy:** The abstract reports 55.2% overall accuracy for the best evaluated model. Your guess of 55.2% is correct.

**Main failure finding:** The authors identify "Implicit Conflict," where a later observation invalidates an earlier memory without explicit negation, so detection requires contextual inference and commonsense reasoning. They report a broad gap between retrieving updated evidence and acting on it. Models often accept outdated assumptions in a user's query, and they struggle to notice when a change in one aspect of the user's state should invalidate related memories.

**CUPMem prototype:** A baseline the authors present for state-aware memory. It strengthens write-time revision through structured state consolidation and propagation-aware search. The authors present it as evidence that explicit state adjudication is a promising direction for agent memory.

**Source:** arXiv:2603.15183, "Token Coherence: Adapting MESI Cache Protocols to Minimize Synchronization Overhead in Multi-Agent LLM Systems." Single author: Vladyslav Parakhin. Submitted March 16, 2026 (cs.DC; v1).

**MESI mapping**
- The paper claims multi-agent LLM synchronization cost maps onto the cache coherence problem in shared-memory multiprocessors, with MESI invalidation transferring to artifact synchronization after minimal structural changes.

**Mechanism**
- Naive broadcast costs scale as O(n × S × |D|) in agents, steps, and artifact size, which the author calls "broadcast-induced triply-multiplicative overhead."
- The proposed Artifact Coherence System (ACS) uses lazy invalidation instead of full-state rebroadcast.
- The stated Token Coherence Theorem reduces cost to O((n + W) × |D|) and gives a savings lower bound of S/(n + W(dᵢ)) when S > n + W(dᵢ).

**Formal verification**
- A TLA+-verified protocol is claimed to enforce single-writer safety, monotonic versioning, and bounded staleness, across about 2,400 explored states.

**Token savings (simulation, four workload configurations)**
- V=0.05: 95.0% ± 1.3%
- V=0.10: 92.3% ± 1.4%
- V=0.25: 88.3% ± 1.5%
- V=0.50: 84.2% ± 1.3%
- V=0.9: about 81%, which the author says contradicts the predicted collapse threshold.

These figures come from simulation, not deployed systems. The paper also claims a reference Python implementation integrating with LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen.

**Author and date:** Walden Yan, published 06.12.25 (June 12, 2025).

**The two principles:**

1. "Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages"
2. "Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results"

**Flappy Bird example:** A task to build a Flappy Bird clone was split into two subtasks: a moving background with green pipes and hitboxes, and a bird that moves up and down. The background subagent misread the goal and built something resembling Super Mario Bros. The bird subagent produced an asset that didn't fit a game and didn't move like Flappy Bird's bird. Even after sharing the original task, the two outputs used conflicting visual styles, because each subagent acted on unstated assumptions.

**Recommended architectures:**

- **Single-threaded linear agent:** Follows both principles by keeping one continuous context. It can overflow on very large tasks.
- **Context compression:** A separate model condenses the history of actions and conversation into key details, events, and decisions. This extends how long an agent can work, though it still has a limit. The author notes this is hard to get right and says Cognition has fine-tuned smaller models for it.

**Claude Code subagents:** As of June 2025, Claude Code's subagents don't run in parallel with the main agent and are usually limited to answering narrow questions rather than writing code. The author attributes this to subagents lacking the main agent's context. Their benefit is keeping investigative work out of the main agent's history, which allows longer traces.

**Edit-apply models:** In 2024, many coding tools had a large model write a markdown description of code changes, which a small model then used to rewrite the file. This was often error-prone because small ambiguities in the instructions led to incorrect edits. Today, a single model usually handles both the decision and the edit.

**Definition**
- The article describes the Contract Net Protocol as "a task-sharing protocol in multi-agent systems, introduced in 1980 by Reid G. Smith." It is used to assign tasks among autonomous agents and resembles sealed-bid auctions.

**Roles**
- **Manager:** Starts the protocol and chooses among proposals. The article says each agent "can be either _manager_ or _contractor_."
- **Contractor:** Responds to a call for proposals with a bid or a refusal, and carries out the awarded task.

**Steps**
1. **Task announcement (call for proposals):** The manager sends a call for proposals to contractors.
2. **Bids:** Interested contractors send a proposal containing the details the manager needs to decide. Others send a refusal.
3. **Award:** The manager accepts the best proposal and rejects the rest.
4. **Result report:** The contractor sends an inform message with any result. If it cannot complete the task, it sends a cancel message.

**Origin**
- Reid G. Smith introduced the protocol in 1980, in a paper in *IEEE Transactions on Computers*.

**Noted weaknesses**
- **Network overload:** Smith proposed short messages and contacting only relevant agents. He also suggested keeping a list of available contractors when many are busy.
- **Limited expressiveness:** The article says "the manager cannot precise what it values most," which can produce suboptimal outcomes. FIPA's iterated version addresses this.
- **No enforced commitment:** The original protocol has contractors commit to a task "whatever it takes," with no sanction for cancelling. Selfish agents may over-bid and drop less profitable tasks. Sandholm and Lesser (1995) proposed a commitment cost for contractors who fail.

**Problem solved:** The algorithm detects termination in a distributed system. The article calls it "an algorithm for detecting termination in a distributed system."

**Termination:** The article doesn't define termination as all processes being passive with no messages in transit. It gives this condition instead: "Termination occurs when the initiator has no children and has become idle." Termination is therefore detected at the root once its subtree of the computation has finished.

**Basic mechanism:**
- **Tree structure:** The initiator is the root. A process that receives a computation message for the first time joins the tree as a child of the sender. Later messages are answered with an acknowledgment, and the article says "the process detaches itself from the tree by sending an acknowledgment message to its tree parent" once it has no children and is idle.
- **Deficit counts:** For directed acyclic graphs, each edge carries a Deficit counter, which is the number of messages received on that edge minus the signals sent back. "Deficit will denote the difference between the number of messages received and the number of signals sent in reply."
- **Cyclic graphs:** The algorithm builds an implicit spanning tree using a First_Edge per node. Each node signals its non-first incoming edges, waits for signals on its outgoing edges, and then signals its First_Edge parent.

**Original reference:**
Dijkstra, Edsger W.; Scholten, C. S. (1980). "Termination detection for diffusing computations." *Information Processing Letters*, 11(1): 1–4. doi:10.1016/0020-0190(80)90021-6

**Definition.** Reason maintenance (also truth maintenance) is an approach to handling inferred information that is not explicitly stored. It separates base facts, which can later be rejected, from derived facts. "Reason maintenance distinguishes between base facts, which can later be rejected, and derived facts." A truth maintenance system (TMS) represents beliefs and their dependencies, and its algorithm maintains those dependencies.

**Justifications and dependencies.** Derived facts are linked to their support through a dependency network. Each node is a knowledge base entry, and each arc records the inference steps by which a node was derived. Premises are assumed true and need no justification. The page lists two justification types: a support list (SL) and conditional proof (CP). Using the current valid premises, the system computes the truth value of derived facts. The article says the system uses this information "to compute the truth value of the stored derived facts and to restore consistency if an inconsistency is derived."

**Retraction and backtracking.** When a contradiction appears, the statements responsible are identified and the records are updated. The page calls this dependency-directed backtracking. It does not describe in detail how retracting a premise propagates to dependent beliefs, so that process isn't covered here.

**JTMS vs. ATMS.** The article does not compare a justification-based TMS (JTMS) with an assumption-based TMS (ATMS). It only says de Kleer's assumption-based TMS (1986) was used in KEE-based systems on Lisp Machines, and it describes single-context and multi-context variants.

**Key references (from the page):**
- Doyle, J. (1979), "A Truth Maintenance System," *AI*, Vol. 12, No. 3, pp. 251–272. The page also cites an earlier MIT technical report, Doyle (1978), AI-TR-419.
- de Kleer, J. (1986), "An assumption-based TMS," *Artificial Intelligence*, 28:127–162.

**Source:** "Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures," published June 10, 2025. Author: Will Fu-Hinthorn (the page header credits "The LangChain Team").

**Setup**
- **Dataset:** A modified τ-bench retail split (first 100 test examples), with six added synthetic "distractor" domains: home improvement, tech support, pharmacy, automotive, restaurant, and Spotify playlist management. Each has 19 tools and a wiki. None are needed to complete the tasks.
- **Model:** gpt-4o for all runs.
- **Architectures:**
  - **Single agent:** one tool-calling agent with access to all domains (the baseline).
  - **Swarm:** agents can hand off to any peer, and responses go directly to the user.
  - **Supervisor:** one agent receives input, delegates to sub-agents, and is the only one that responds to the user.

**Scores**
- The single agent drops sharply with two or more distractor domains. With one distractor, it performs slightly better than the others.
- Swarm slightly outperforms supervisor across the board.
- The text doesn't give exact numeric scores, and the metric is left unspecified.

**Token usage**
- Single-agent token use rises consistently as distractor domains increase.
- Supervisor and swarm stay roughly flat.
- Supervisor uses more tokens than swarm throughout, which the author attributes to translation.

**Why supervisor underperforms**
- Sub-agents can't talk to the user directly, so the supervisor relays their output. The author compares this to a "game of telephone," where meaning degrades in translation.

**Supervisor improvements**
- **Removing handoff messages:** Sub-agents no longer see routing logic, which reduces context clutter.
- **`forward_message` tool:** The supervisor can pass a sub-agent's response through without regenerating it, reducing paraphrasing errors.
- **Tool naming:** The author tested "delegate_to_<agent>" against "transfer_to_<agent>."
- **Result:** The article's introduction reports a "nearly 50% increase in performance on this benchmark." The old-versus-new comparison is charted, but the chart values aren't in the text. The changes are included in the latest `langgraph_supervisor`.

**Recommendations**
- Start from your goals and constraints. Some architectures may be infeasible: swarm requires every agent to know the others, and a single agent can't use third-party sub-agents.
- Supervisor makes the fewest assumptions about sub-agents, so it's the most broadly feasible generic option.
- Improve how information passes between sub-agents and the user, and how context is managed.
- Evaluate on your own data, with a tool like LangSmith.
- The author expects multi-agent systems to become more common, and generic architectures to become reliable enough as models improve.

**Open questions (future work)**
- Performance on multi-hop questions requiring several sub-agents.
- Closing the gap with the single agent when only one distractor domain is present.
- Reducing or skipping the translation layer.
- Comparing against other approaches, such as "agents-as-tools."

**Definition**
- A blackboard system is an AI approach in which a shared "blackboard" knowledge base is updated by specialist knowledge sources. The article says each one adds a partial solution "when its internal constraints match the blackboard state" (the quoted text is 104 characters).

**Three components**
1. **Knowledge sources (KSs):** specialist modules, each providing a specific expertise the application needs.
2. **Blackboard:** a shared repository of problems, partial solutions, suggestions, and contributed information, which the article describes as a dynamic "library" of recent contributions.
3. **Control shell:** manages the flow of problem-solving. The article says KSs "need a mechanism to organize their use in the most effective and coherent fashion" (87 characters), and that the control shell provides it.

**Opportunistic triggering**
- The article's metaphor describes specialists watching the blackboard and contributing when something written there lets them apply their expertise. Each contribution can enable others.
- It attributes this opportunistic style to Hayes-Roth & Hayes-Roth's model of human planning, quoting: "the planner's current decisions and observations suggest various opportunities for plan development" (99 characters).
- It notes that ACCORD-style frameworks use "events to trigger KSes" and "preconditions to run a KS action."

**Control choosing which KS runs**
- The article does not explicitly say the control shell picks the next KS to run. It does describe BB1, where control was itself handled by the blackboard model, with meta-level control knowledge sources that monitor progress. If planning stalled, BB1 "could switch from one strategy to another" (58 characters).
- GBB1 is described as a control shell that implements BB1-style control with efficiency improvements.

**Hearsay-II origin**
- The article lists Hearsay II, a speech recognition system, among the well-known early academic blackboard systems.
- Its only dated reference is Erman, Hayes-Roth, Lesser & Reddy (1980), "The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System," in *ACM Computing Surveys*. The article gives no other origin dates.

73	- Follow the search hints a website gives. If a search returns nothing or too much, change the search terms.
74	- When a question asks for every item in a list, inspect its page controls and use collect on the control that
75	  advances that list before filing it. Check the resulting page count or end state; do not mark a list complete after
76	  seeing only its first page. If the list is inside an embedded document, use the controls belonging to that document.
77	- For mailbox questions, search relevant folders separately when mailbox search covers only the current folder;
78	  include the archive when looking for historical or latest records. If a query is too broad or returns nothing,
79	  refine the terms and try again. Open candidate messages and file the message itself, not only its hit row.
80	- If the news says extraction failed or found no usable records, do not mark that question complete. Reopen the
81	  evidence page, check that it contains the records requested, and file it again with the right kind.
82	- When no open question is left that your website can answer right now, finish with done, also when you need
83	  facts the other agents have not filed yet. You are called again as soon as the case file brings new questions.

92	    def __init__(self, case: CaseFile, names: list[str], deadline: float):

97	    def hook(self, name: str):
98	        async def hold(why: str) -> str | None:
99	            version = self.case.version
100	            before = {qid for qid, _ in self.case.questions()}
101	            self.idle.add(name)
102	            try:
103	                while not self.finished.is_set() and time.time() < self.deadline:
104	                    changed = await self.case.wait_change(version, 1.0)
105	                    if self.finished.is_set():
106	                        break
107	                    if changed:
108	                        version = self.case.version
109	                        fresh = {qid for qid, _ in self.case.questions()} - before
110	                        if fresh or self.case.news.get(name):
111	                            return "The case file has news" + (f"; new open questions: {', '.join(sorted(fresh))}" if fresh else "") + "."
112	                    elif self.idle == self.names and self.case.pending == 0:
113	                        self.finished.set()
114	                return None
115	            finally:
116	                self.idle.discard(name)
117	        return hold

256	def _merge(store: dict, key, record: dict) -> list[tuple[str, object, object]]:
257	    """The value filed last is the one in use. Returns where it replaced a different one, as (field, earlier,
258	    later): two documents that disagree about the same record are a conflict to report, not to overwrite in
259	    silence (a draft, a superseded revision and a look-alike record all look like this)."""
260	    old = store.setdefault(key, {})
261	    replaced = []
262	    for name, value in record.items():
263	        if value is not None and value != "" and value != []:
264	            earlier = old.get(name)
265	            if earlier is not None and name not in QUIET_FIELDS and not same_value(earlier, value):
266	                replaced.append((name, earlier, value))
267	            old[name] = value
268	    return replaced

61	    """A stable signature of the model-visible page state.

63	    ``Tab.observe`` assigns fresh action ids on every read.  They are useful to
