# Coordination and routing for parallel LLM agents that gather interdependent facts under a hard deadline (as of October 2026)

Reading guide. Evidence grades used below: **[read]** = the page was fetched and read in this session; **[abstract]** = only the abstract or landing page was read; **[search]** = seen only as a search-result summary, not opened (treat as a lead, not as a verified fact). Statements are paraphrased; there is one short verbatim quote (MetaGPT, section 3). Everything under "Inferences" is my reasoning, not a reported result. Section 7 contains the concrete designs and pseudocode; none of them has been measured. References to `starter-kit/*.py` are observations of the existing code in this repository.

---

## 1. Orchestrator-worker versus peer blackboard versus hybrid: what do published systems use, and what does the evidence say for information gathering with dependencies?

### Takeaway
Published systems split into (a) an LLM orchestrator that plans and delegates (Anthropic Research, Magentic-One, LangGraph supervisor, OpenAI agents-as-tools), (b) peer handoff (LangGraph swarm, OpenAI handoffs) and (c) a shared typed state with subscription or volunteering (MetaGPT message pool, the 2025 LLM blackboard papers). The evidence favours parallel workers only for the independent part of the work, a shared state rather than relayed messages for the dependent part, and some explicit control logic (ledger, stall counter, verification) on top; no source measured an LLM orchestrator beating deterministic control code on a task whose open sub-questions can be derived mechanically.

### Cited Findings

Orchestrator-worker systems
- Anthropic's Research feature is an orchestrator-worker system: a lead agent plans, spawns subagents that search in parallel, then synthesises; a separate citation pass follows. [read] — [Anthropic, "How we built our multi-agent research system"](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Reported gain: lead Claude Opus 4 with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal research evaluation; multi-agent runs use about 15 times the tokens of a chat; on BrowseComp three factors explain 95% of the variance and token usage alone explains 80%. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Stated limits of that design: the lead waits synchronously for each batch of subagents, cannot steer them while they run, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and one slow subagent can hold up the whole system; asynchronous execution is named as future work because it raises result-coordination, state-consistency and error-propagation problems. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Stated poor fits: domains where all agents need the same context, tasks with many dependencies between agents, and real-time coordination between agents. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Vague delegation produced duplicated work and gaps (example in the post: one subagent on the 2021 chip crisis while two others repeated the same 2025 supply-chain searches); the fix was a task description with objective, output format, tool and source guidance and explicit boundaries. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Subagents can write results to an external store and hand the lead only a lightweight reference, which reduces information loss from relaying. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Magentic-One: one Orchestrator keeps a task ledger (verified facts, facts to look up, facts to derive, educated guesses, plan) and a progress ledger that it rewrites every step by answering five questions: is the request satisfied, is the team looping, is progress being made, who acts next, with what instruction. [read] — [Fourney et al., Magentic-One, arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Magentic-One keeps a stall counter (threshold 2 in the experiments); above it the Orchestrator reflects, rewrites the task ledger and the plan, and every agent's context is cleared. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Ablation on GAIA validation (GPT-4o): replacing the ledger Orchestrator with a simple group-chat style one (no ledgers, no progress tracking, no loop detection) costs 31% of performance; removing a single worker costs 21% to 39%. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Magentic-One absolute level: GAIA test 32.33% (GPT-4o) and 38.00% (GPT-4o + o1), WebArena 32.8%; human GAIA 92%. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Microsoft Agent Framework ships the same pattern as "Magentic" orchestration with explicit knobs `max_round_count`, `max_stall_count`, `max_reset_count`; consecutive rounds without progress raise a stall counter and exceeding the maximum triggers a reset and a new plan. [read, documentation excerpt] — [Microsoft Learn, Agent Framework: Magentic orchestration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/orchestrations/magentic)
- OpenAI Agents SDK documents two orchestration styles: by LLM (the model plans, uses tools, hands off) and by code, and states that orchestration by code makes speed, cost and performance more deterministic and predictable; it recommends `asyncio.gather` for tasks that do not depend on each other and a `while` loop with an evaluator until criteria are met. [read] — [OpenAI Agents SDK, "Orchestrating multiple agents"](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/)
- OpenAI Agents SDK distinguishes handoffs (a triage agent passes the conversation to a specialist who then owns the turn) from agents-as-tools (a manager keeps control and calls specialists). [read] — [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/)

Supervisor versus swarm (LangGraph)
- LangChain benchmark (10 June 2025, gpt-4o, modified tau-bench retail plus up to six irrelevant "distractor" domains of 19 tools each): the single agent degrades sharply with two or more distractor domains; swarm slightly outperforms supervisor at every size; supervisor spends more tokens because it re-words what sub-agents said (the author calls this a game of telephone). Exact scores are only in charts. [read] — [LangChain, "Benchmarking Multi-Agent Architectures"](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)
- Three changes to the supervisor (hide handoff messages from sub-agents, a `forward_message` tool that passes a sub-agent's reply through unchanged, different handoff tool naming) raised its score by nearly 50% on that benchmark. [read] — [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)
- Constraint noted there: a swarm requires every agent to know every other agent; a supervisor makes the fewest assumptions about sub-agents. [read] — [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)
- LangGraph implements both with the `Command` primitive (a node returns a state update plus the next node); in the swarm an `active_agent` field in the shared state records who runs next. [search] — [LangChain docs, multi-agent prebuilts](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/multi-agent-prebuilts)
- CrewAI Flows are event-driven: `@start()` methods run (possibly in parallel) at kickoff, `@listen()` methods fire on another method's output, and all methods read and write one typed (Pydantic) state object. [search] — [CrewAI docs, Flows](https://docs.crewai.com/en/concepts/flows)

Shared pool and blackboard systems
- MetaGPT replaces dialogue with a shared message pool and publish-subscribe: agents publish structured documents, each role subscribes to the message types it cares about, and a role acts only when its prerequisites are present; reported pass@1 85.9% (HumanEval) and 87.7% (MBPP). Background, 2023-2024. [read] — [Hong et al., MetaGPT, arXiv 2308.00352](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00352v7)
- Google/UMass blackboard system for information discovery (October 2025): a main agent posts a request to a shared blackboard without addressing anyone; helper agents (one per partition of a data lake, plus a web-search agent) watch the board and decide by themselves whether to answer; answers go to a separate response board that only the main agent reads, so helpers do not influence each other. [read] — [Salemi et al., arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- The paper's stated motivation: a master-slave controller needs precise knowledge of what each sub-agent can do, which it does not have when it cannot see inside the sub-agents' data. [abstract] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01285)
- Results (end-to-end success, macro average over KramaBench, DSBench, DA-Code): blackboard 28.53 vs master-slave 24.01 vs RAG 18.51 with Gemini 2.5 Pro; 31.43 vs 27.63 vs 23.00 with Claude 4 Opus; 7.90 vs 5.03 vs 3.87 with Qwen3-Coder; the paper summarises this as 13% to 57% relative improvement. File-discovery F1 with Gemini 2.5 Pro: 0.561 vs 0.513 (master-slave) vs 0.247 (RAG). [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- Cost of that blackboard: about 1.8 times master-slave and 2.3 times RAG per question; not every cell is a win (for example master-slave beats blackboard on two KramaBench domains with Qwen3-Coder and with Claude 4 Opus). [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- LbMAS (July 2025): a blackboard with public and private spaces; an LLM control unit picks which agents act each round from the query, the board's content and the agents' described abilities; fixed roles include planner, critic, decider, conflict-resolver and cleaner. Average score 81.68 vs 80.56 for the best listed baseline on reasoning and maths sets. [read] — [Han and Zhang, arXiv 2507.01701](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)
- LbMAS ablation: letting agents decide for themselves without the control unit raised token use on MATH from 4.72M to 13.86M with only slight score changes. [read] — [arXiv 2507.01701](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)

Cross-architecture evidence
- Google/MIT scaling study (December 2025, revised April 2026): 260 configurations, six agentic benchmarks, three model families, five architectures (single, independent, centralized, decentralized, hybrid). Multi-agent change against single agent ranges from +80.8% on a decomposable financial-reasoning task to -70.0% on sequential planning; architectures without centralized verification propagate errors more; a predictive model picks the best architecture for 87% of held-out configurations. [abstract, v3] — [Kim et al., "Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems", arXiv 2512.08296](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296)
- Cognition's counter-position (12 June 2025): share full context and full traces rather than single messages, and remember that every action embeds decisions, so parallel agents with separate contexts make conflicting ones (their example: a Flappy Bird clone whose background and bird, built by two subagents, did not match). [read] — [Walden Yan, "Don't Build Multi-Agents"](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents)
- Background (classic): a blackboard system has three parts, the shared blackboard, specialist knowledge sources that contribute when the board's state matches their conditions, and a control shell that organises their use; Hearsay-II (Erman et al., 1980) is the canonical example; BB1 put control knowledge on the board itself and could switch strategy when planning stalled. [read] — [Wikipedia, Blackboard system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard_system)

### Inferences
- The system described in the brief is already a blackboard system in the classic sense: the case file is the blackboard, each site investigator is a knowledge source, `CaseFile.questions()` plus `Team` is the control shell. The four observed failures (blind search, stale rejection, one-folder search, missed wake-up) are control-shell failures, not signs that the architecture is wrong. Switching to an LLM orchestrator would add a relay layer (LangChain's "telephone" loss), a 3-second serial call on the critical path, and the synchronous-wait weakness Anthropic describes, while the thing an orchestrator contributes (knowing what is missing) is already computed deterministically.
- Recommended shape: **blackboard + deterministic control shell + one LLM worker per source**. Take from Magentic-One the ledger and the stall counter, but compute them in code from the case file; take from the Google blackboard paper the volunteering (workers decide whether a request fits their source); take from MetaGPT the subscription and prerequisite gating; take from the LangChain result the narrowing of each agent's view (irrelevant questions in context cost accuracy, which matches the measured 100-point "own questions only" variant).
- The Google scaling numbers and Anthropic's "poor fit" list both say the same thing for this task: parallelise fact gathering per source, keep the dependent, sequential part (rule application, form fill, signing) single-threaded and deterministic.
- Cognition's second principle is exactly the stale-rejection failure: the ERP agent's rejection was an implicit decision taken on a value another agent later changed. A shared state fixes context sharing but not decision invalidation; that needs section 4.
- The 31% Magentic-One ablation and the 3x token cost in the LbMAS ablation are the best available evidence that explicit control beats free-running agents. Neither compares LLM control with deterministic control; that deterministic control is at least as good when the open questions are mechanically derivable is my inference.

### Gaps
- AutoGen's original group chat (LLM speaker selection) and its successors were not read directly; the only evidence used is Magentic-One's ablation against a group-chat style orchestrator and the Microsoft Agent Framework documentation excerpt.
- CrewAI Flows and LangGraph `Command` are cited from documentation search summaries only; `@router` semantics were not verified.
- The scaling paper's per-architecture error-amplification factors and its numeric saturation threshold are not in the abstract and were not verified.
- No source found that evaluates orchestrator vs blackboard on multi-site web navigation with a wall-clock deadline; all transfers to that setting are inference.

---

## 2. Capability discovery and dynamic routing: how can a system learn at run time which source answers which kind of question?

### Takeaway
The best-supported pattern is decentralised volunteering after a cheap profiling pass: each worker inspects its own source, describes what it holds, and decides per request whether it can contribute, which beat a central router that had to guess (13% to 57% relative). No published system measures missed questions or double work under a wrong profile, so safe degradation has to be designed in: treat the profile as a prior, let evidence of where records were actually found override it, and never let a question stay invisible.

### Cited Findings
- In the Google blackboard system each file agent first profiles its partition offline (opens some or all files, learns structure and needed preprocessing); online it answers a posted request only if it judges the request relevant, returning the files, loading code and samples. The web-search agent first checks feasibility and declines requests that need local files. [read] — [Salemi et al., arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- That paper has no confidence score in the volunteering step and reports no statistics on requests nobody answered, on wrong volunteers or on duplicate answers; its case study shows 3 of 8 helpers responding to one request. [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- Volunteering versus central assignment in that paper: file-discovery F1 0.561 (blackboard) vs 0.513 (master-slave) vs 0.247 (RAG) with Gemini 2.5 Pro; relative gain over master-slave grows with the size of the source pool (70% at 145 files, 211% at 1,556 files). [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- More and better partitions help: clustering by content beats clustering by file name, and more clusters generally improve results (2 to 16 tested). [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- Unrestricted self-selection is expensive: in LbMAS, agents choosing by themselves when to act (no control unit) used about three times the tokens (13.86M vs 4.72M on MATH) for little change in score. [read] — [Han and Zhang, arXiv 2507.01701](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)
- Irrelevant material in an agent's context hurts: the single agent in LangChain's benchmark drops sharply once two or more unrelated domains are in its prompt, while agents scoped to one domain keep roughly flat token use. [read] — [LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)
- Without explicit boundaries parallel workers duplicate each other and leave gaps (Anthropic's delegation lesson). [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- Agent-written site knowledge transfers to unseen websites: Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable workflows from experience, also online from the test queries themselves; reported relative success gains of 24.6% (Mind2Web) and 51.1% (WebArena), fewer steps on WebArena, and an advantage that grows from 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as test sites move further from training sites. [abstract] — [Wang et al., arXiv 2409.07429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)
- Background (classic): in the contract net protocol (Smith, 1980) a manager announces a task, contractors bid or refuse, the manager awards, the contractor reports a result or cancels. Known weaknesses: message overload, bids that cannot express what the manager values, and no penalty for a contractor that over-bids and then drops the task. [read] — [Wikipedia, Contract Net Protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_Net_Protocol)
- An LLM-assisted contract-net scheduler (2026) keeps measurements, hard constraints and numeric ranking deterministic and uses the LLM only to interpret and to write proposals; negotiation stops when one feasible candidate remains, a stable best emerges or a round limit is hit. [search] — [arXiv 2608.12371](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.12371)
- COALESCE (2025) notes that auction-style task outsourcing among LLM agents is hard because outcomes are uncertain and skills are not scalar. [search] — [arXiv 2506.01900](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.01900)
- Google's A2A protocol publishes capabilities as an Agent Card (JSON at a well-known URL) whose `skills` entries carry id, name, description and tags; clients read the card to decide what to send where. [search, secondary source] — [Tyk, A2A protocol: architecture and technical specification](https://tyk.io/learning-center/a2a-protocol-architecture-and-technical-specification/)

[search] — [RAGRoute, arXiv 2502.19280](https://papers.cool/arxiv/2502.19280); [Cohere docs, routing queries to data sources](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/routing-queries-to-data-sources); [arXiv 2510.02388](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.02388)

- Magentic-One's ablation notes that when a specialist was removed, the remaining agents sometimes covered the missing capability by other means. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)

### Inferences
- What can go wrong, by mechanism:
  - *Hiding by profile* (questions shown only to the believed owner): a wrong or incomplete profile makes a question invisible to the only agent that could answer it. This is the failure mode with unbounded cost (missed fact, not just wasted turns).
  - *Broadcast* (everyone sees everything): no missed questions, but double work and, worse, agents trying to answer on a source that cannot hold the fact (the 45-turn blind search), plus the context-dilution effect LangChain measured.
  - *Self-claiming with a weak model*: a fast non-thinking model tends to over-claim; contract net has no built-in penalty for that.
  - *Split information*: evidence that source A holds records of a type does not prove that source B holds none.
- Design principle that degrades safely: **profile as prior, provenance as posterior, lease as safety net.** A site card written by the agent after a first look gives the initial claim; the first record of a given type actually extracted from an agent's filing overrides claims; a question nobody advances within a lease is widened step by step until every agent sees it. Under a wrong profile the worst case is then a delay of one lease, not a missed fact; under a right profile the system behaves like the measured "own questions only" variant.
- The routing key must be the *kind of fact the question needs* (a property of the rules and the case-file schema), never the site name. The site-to-kind relation is the only thing learned at run time. Concrete design in section 7.2.
- Claims should be grounded: require the agent to cite the label or text on its site that supports a claim, and check deterministically that this text occurs on a page it saw. This is my proposal, analogous to the existing extraction grounding; no source measured it.
- "Absent" must be scoped to the source: an agent that cannot find something has shown only that it is not on its own site. Treating that as a disclaimer (routing evidence) instead of a global close is what makes dynamic routing safe.

### Gaps
- No published measurement of missed-question or duplicate-work rates for volunteering or bidding schemes was found; the Google paper does not report them.
- No evidence was found on the calibration of confidence-stamped claims from small, non-thinking models.
- A2A, RAGRoute, the Cohere guide and the two contract-net papers were seen only as search summaries; the arXiv identifier 2608.12371 should be re-checked before it is cited in a report.
- No source evaluates "site cards" for multi-agent routing specifically; AWM supports only the weaker claim that agent-written site knowledge helps a single agent on unseen sites.

## 3. Dependency-aware scheduling: task graphs, releasing a question only when its inputs are stable, speculative work, and what to do while blocked

### Takeaway
Planner-compiler systems (LLMCompiler, ReWOO) and MetaGPT all dispatch a dependent step only after its inputs exist, and get their speed from running the independent steps at once; none of them models inputs that exist but may still be revised. For that case the literature offers replanning after the fact rather than stability gating, so the "tentative" state and the behaviour of a blocked agent have to be designed, not copied.

### Cited Findings
- LLMCompiler: a planner emits a DAG of tasks with dependencies; a Task Fetching Unit dispatches each task as soon as its dependencies are resolved and substitutes the placeholder variables with real results; an executor runs ready tasks in parallel; when intermediate results change the picture, results go back to the planner for a new plan. Reported latency speedup up to 3.7 times against ReAct. Background, 2023-2024. [read, paper excerpt and ICML abstract] — [Kim et al., arXiv 2312.04511](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511); [ICML 2024 poster](https://icml.cc/virtual/2024/poster/32829)
- ReWOO separates planning from observation: the whole plan is written first with references to results that do not exist yet, then tools run, then a final step combines; reported 5 times token efficiency and 4% higher accuracy on HotpotQA, and robustness when a tool fails. Background, 2023. [abstract] — [Xu et al., arXiv 2305.18323](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18323)
- MetaGPT gates actions on inputs: "an agent activates its action only after receiving all its prerequisite dependencies". [read] — [Hong et al., arXiv 2308.00352](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00352v7)
- Magentic-One's task ledger separates verified facts, facts to look up, facts to derive and educated guesses before any plan is made, and the plan is treated as a hint that is rewritten when progress stalls. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- In the Google blackboard system the main agent posts a request at the moment it needs data, and helpers answer with a ready-to-use plan (files, loading code, samples) rather than raw content. [read] — [arXiv 2510.01285](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)
- Anthropic's search guidance is to start with short, broad queries and narrow afterwards, and to scale effort to the query (1 agent and 3 to 10 calls for a simple fact, more than 10 subagents only for complex research). [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- OpenAI's guidance limits parallel execution to tasks that do not depend on each other. [read] — [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/)
- Sequential, dependent tasks are where multi-agent setups lose most (down to -70.0% against a single agent in the Google scaling study). [abstract] — [arXiv 2512.08296](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296)
- The most common error theme in Magentic-One's logs is agents persisting with unproductive actions; inefficient navigation attempts is the third. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Workflows learned on a site shorten later tasks on the same site (AWM reduces steps on WebArena). [abstract] — [arXiv 2409.07429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07429)

### Inferences
- The existing `CaseFile.questions()` is already a dynamic task graph in the LLMCompiler sense: `material:R` is emitted only when requirement R is complete, `reserve:R` only when R needs one, `data:M` only once a material matched. What it lacks is a third state between "blocked" and "ready".
- Proposed three states per question, all derivable without site knowledge:
  - **BLOCKED**: an input fact is missing. Not shown (already the case).
  - **TENTATIVE**: inputs are present, but something that can still revise them is unfinished: an upstream question of the kinds that feed these inputs is still open, or an extraction of such a kind is pending. Shown with a marker and a restricted contract: gather the superset, do not conclude.
  - **READY**: inputs present and their upstream questions closed. Full contract, "absent" allowed.
- Speculative work that survives a correction is *superset retrieval keyed on the most stable attribute*. For the material example: file every material of the catalogue group (stable) instead of searching for one bore/stroke/pressure combination (volatile); the deterministic matcher then picks the right one whenever the values settle. This turns the later correction from a 46-turn failure into a zero-turn non-event, because the candidate is already on file.
- What a blocked agent should do, in order of value: (1) a bounded first look that produces a site card (sections, search facilities, record types, which identifiers are searchable), which is also the routing input of section 2; (2) nothing, i.e. sleep until woken. Blind item-level searching without inputs has no upside and was the measured 45-turn failure. Pre-fetching bulk lists is only worth it if the site card says the list is small; I found no measurement for this.
- A turn budget is the deterministic backstop: an agent with no READY or TENTATIVE question routed to it gets at most N survey turns, then is held. This is scheduling, which the competition rules leave to code; what to open during the survey stays the model's choice.
- Stability by quiet period alone (value unchanged for X seconds) is fragile because arrival order is exactly what varied between the 100-point and 10-point runs. Tying stability to the closure of upstream questions is order-independent.

### Gaps
- No published system was found that gates work on input *stability* (as opposed to input existence) or that measures speculative pre-work for LLM information-gathering agents. A 2025 paper on speculative actions for faster agent systems exists to my recollection, but it was not retrieved or verified in this session.
- LLMCompiler's detailed benchmark numbers were only partly legible in the excerpt; only the abstract-level speedup is cited.
- The LangChain overview of plan-and-execute variants could not be read (redirect not followed).

## 4. Stale beliefs: how do multi-agent systems propagate state changes?

### Takeaway
Current LLM work mostly re-reads the shared state every turn and marks older entries as superseded; push notification and automatic invalidation of derived conclusions are rare, and benchmarks show that models often keep acting on an outdated premise even when the new value is retrievable (best model 55.2% on STALE). The classic answer, truth maintenance, translates directly and cheaply: record what each conclusion depended on, and when a premise changes, retract the conclusions and tell their owners.

### Cited Findings
- "Stale propagation" is named as one of four fleet-memory failure modes (with unauthorised leakage, contradiction persistence and provenance collapse): one agent updates a value while another still reads the old one. [read] — [Margalit et al., "Governed Shared Memory for Multi-Agent LLM Systems", arXiv 2606.24535](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.24535v1)
- That system's remedy is temporal supersession (the older row is marked outdated and linked from the newer one via a supersedes id), a structural contradiction detector on single-valued predicates, and provenance fields (writer, source system, derived-from). It has no subscription or push mechanism; propagation is measured by polling search. [read] — [arXiv 2606.24535](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.24535v1)
- Its measured results (authors' own live system, no baseline): 0 stale reads in 200 fact runs, supersession established within about 6 seconds, contradiction detected in 90 of 90 cases where both writes were admitted, but a duplicate filter rejected 206 of 400 writes before detection. [read] — [arXiv 2606.24535](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.24535v1)
- STALE benchmark (May 2026): 400 conflict scenarios, 1,200 queries, three probes (recognise that a belief is outdated, resist a query that presupposes the old state, apply the new state in later behaviour). Best model 55.2% overall. Models struggle most when a change in one aspect should invalidate related memories without being stated, and there is a gap between retrieving the new evidence and acting on it. The authors' prototype improves this by revising at write time and consolidating state explicitly. Single-agent. [abstract] — [Chao et al., arXiv 2605.06527](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527)
- BeliefTrack (May 2026) separates three belief failures: failing to keep a belief, failing to update it, and failing to isolate it. [search] — [arXiv 2605.30219](https://papers.cool/arxiv/2605.30219)
- "Token Coherence" (March 2026, single author, simulation only) maps multi-agent synchronisation onto cache coherence: instead of re-broadcasting full state, invalidate on write and fetch lazily; a TLA+ model is claimed to enforce single-writer safety, monotonic versions and bounded staleness; simulated token savings of 84% to 95%. [abstract] — [Parakhin, arXiv 2603.15183](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15183)
- A March 2026 position paper treats multi-agent memory as a computer-architecture problem and names consistency as the most pressing open issue. [search] — [arXiv 2603.10062](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.10062v1)
- Magentic-One's answer to drift is re-grounding: on a stall it rewrites the task ledger and clears every agent's context before continuing. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- LbMAS manages board content actively: a conflict-resolver agent names contradicting messages and their authors, and a cleaner agent removes redundant messages; removing them scored better than merely marking them (72.60 vs 71.00 on MATH). [read] — [Han and Zhang, arXiv 2507.01701](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)
- Anthropic names state consistency as an open problem of asynchronous subagents and notes that errors compound in stateful agents. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- MAST lists memory and state management as a structural mitigation that is still mostly studied for single agents, and measures "ignored other agent's input" at 1.9% and "loss of conversation history" at 2.8% of failures. [read] — [Cemri et al., arXiv 2503.13657](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)
- Background (classic): a truth maintenance system separates premises from derived facts, stores for each derived fact the justification it rests on, recomputes derived facts from the currently valid premises and restores consistency when a contradiction appears (dependency-directed backtracking). Doyle 1979; de Kleer's assumption-based variant 1986. [read] — [Wikipedia, Reason maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance)
- Background (classic): in blackboard frameworks knowledge sources are triggered by events on the board and run when their preconditions hold. [read] — [Wikipedia, Blackboard system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard_system)

### Inferences
- Why "the agent sees the full case file every turn" was not enough in the measured runs (observations of the code plus STALE's finding):
  1. Re-grounding was present but not salient: the corrected value appeared inside a regenerated question text, with no marker that it had changed. STALE shows that models often keep the old premise in exactly this situation.
  2. The agent's own earlier reasoning stays in its context: `Agent._messages` in `starter-kit/worker.py` keeps every past assistant reply, including thoughts that state the old value, so the context contains more copies of the old value than of the new one.
  3. Derived conclusions are not tied to their premises: `CaseFile.answers` in `starter-kit/casefile.py` closes a question by id only, so an "absent" given under the old requirement value survives the correction.
  4. Notification is edge-triggered on question ids and addressed only to the filer: `Team.hook` in `starter-kit/agent.py` wakes an idle agent on a new id or on news about its own filings; a changed question with an unchanged id wakes nobody.
- Three layers, cheapest first (design in 7.1 and 7.4):
  - **Basis stamps (truth maintenance, minimal form).** Every question carries a hash of the input values it was derived from. Every conclusion an agent can record (answer "absent", "not on my site", a give-up at `done`) stores the basis it was made under. A conclusion counts only while its basis equals the current one. This retracts stale conclusions automatically and without any LLM call.
  - **Push with a diff.** When a merge changes a value that some open question depends on, every agent that can see that question gets a short CHANGED line (old value, new value, which document) ahead of the case summary, and idle agents are woken.
  - **Context hygiene.** On a CHANGED notice that touches the agent's questions, drop the free-text thoughts from older turns and keep only the action log. Keeping what was done while dropping what was concluded mirrors the premise/derived split of a truth maintenance system and Magentic-One's context reset.
- Where selection can be computed, keep it out of the model: the existing deterministic matcher already decides which material fits; the agent's job is to file candidates. The more of the judgement is deterministic and recomputed from current facts, the fewer beliefs exist that can go stale.
- "Value filed last wins" (`_merge`) is the weakest part of supersession: a late-arriving superseded document would overwrite the right value. Authority (status, revision, date) should decide, with arrival order only as a tie-break; the existing conflict list is the hook for that. This sits at the edge of this note's scope.

### Gaps
- No peer-reviewed measurement was found of push notification versus per-turn re-reading for multi-agent LLM systems; the two 2026 papers closest to the topic are a vendor self-evaluation and a single-author simulation.
- No published evidence that stripping an agent's earlier reasoning from context improves belief updating; the recommendation rests on STALE's findings and on Magentic-One's reset practice.
- BeliefTrack and the architecture position paper were seen only as search summaries.

## 6. Wake-up and termination: how to decide the team is done without stopping early or waiting idle

### Takeaway
Published systems let an LLM decide completion and bound it with counters (rounds, stalls, resets, time); MAST shows that this is where about one failure in five sits (12.4% unaware of termination, 6.2% premature termination). With a typed case file the decision can be made in code: finish when no required fact is missing, otherwise when every agent is idle, nothing is in flight and every remaining question has been given up under its current inputs by every agent that could see it, otherwise at a deadline reserve.

### Cited Findings
- Magentic-One ends when the Orchestrator judges the request satisfied or when configured limits hit (maximum attempts or time, 25 minutes given as an example); at the end it reports a final answer or its best guess. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Microsoft Agent Framework exposes the bounds explicitly (maximum rounds, stalls, resets); the progress ledger's fields are: request satisfied, in a loop, progress being made, next speaker, instruction. [read, documentation excerpt] — [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/workflows/orchestrations/magentic)
- LbMAS stops when a decider agent finds enough on the board or after 4 rounds, then falls back to a similarity vote; the agents reached consensus in 89.8% (MMLU), 52.5% (GPQA) and 29.4% (MATH) of cases, so the round limit did much of the stopping on hard tasks. [read] — [Han and Zhang, arXiv 2507.01701](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01701)
- MAST: unaware of termination conditions 12.4%, premature termination 6.2%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%; adding a high-level objective check and a cyclic topology raised ChatDev from 25.0 to 40.6 on ProgramDev. [read] — [arXiv 2503.13657](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)
- Anthropic's lead agent decides after each batch whether more research is needed and can spawn more subagents; its synchronous design can stall on one slow subagent. [read] — [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- OpenAI recommends an evaluator in a `while` loop that runs until stated criteria are met as a code-orchestrated stop rule. [read] — [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/multi_agent/)
- Insufficient verification before declaring completion is the second most common error theme in Magentic-One's logs. [read] — [arXiv 2411.04468](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)
- Background (classic): termination detection for a diffusing distributed computation (Dijkstra and Scholten, 1980) needs more than "every process is idle"; it tracks outstanding messages per edge (a deficit count) so that work still in transit is not missed. [read] — [Wikipedia, Dijkstra-Scholten algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%E2%80%93Scholten_algorithm)
- Background (classic): BB1 placed control knowledge on the blackboard and switched strategy when progress stalled. [read] — [Wikipedia, Blackboard system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackboard_system)

### Inferences
- The existing rule in `starter-kit/agent.py` (`Team`: finish when every agent is idle and `case.pending == 0`) is the correct quiescence condition in the Dijkstra-Scholten sense, because pending extractions are the only messages in transit. Two things are missing around it: a positive completion test (stop as soon as nothing is missing, without waiting for every agent to say done) and a last check that no open question was abandoned by mistake.
- Wake-up should be level-triggered, not edge-triggered. Edge: "a question id I have not seen appeared". Level: "there is a question visible to me whose current basis I have not given up on". The level form covers all the missed cases at once: corrected inputs under an unchanged id, a question newly routed to me by escalation, a question reopened because the answer that closed it lost its basis.
- An agent's `done` should mean "I have nothing I can do now", stay reversible (sleep), and record which question versions it is giving up on. Global completion is decided by code from the case file. This removes MAST modes 1.5 and 3.1 from the model's responsibility.
- Before quiescent termination with open questions, one bounded "last call" per question to agents that have not explicitly given up on its current version is cheap insurance against a routing error; bounded by a counter so that it cannot loop.
- A deadline reserve (time to calculate, fill and sign, measured from the good runs plus margin) should pre-empt everything; a partially supported bid that is signed beats a complete one that is not.
- A stall counter per agent (no change of the case file caused by this agent, and no new page or query in its coverage record, for K turns) addresses "45 turns" and "46 turns" directly; the first stall injects a notice with the current inputs, the second forces a hold and widens the question to other agents. Threshold 2 is Magentic-One's setting; K is a guess (6 to 8 turns).

### Gaps
- No published comparison of LLM-decided versus state-derived termination was found.
- No source gives guidance on choosing the stall threshold in turns for web navigation; Magentic-One's threshold counts orchestrator rounds, not worker turns.

## 7. Concrete designs that fit the existing Python system and can be built in a few hours

### Takeaway
Six small, deterministic changes to `casefile.py`, `agent.py`, `worker.py` and `coverage.py` cover all four measured failures and replace site-name routing with routing learned at run time; the first two (basis stamps with level-triggered wake, and change push) are about an hour of work and fix the two failures that cost the most turns. Everything below is my design, derived from the evidence in sections 1 to 6 and from reading the code; none of it has been run.

### Cited Findings
Observations of the existing code that the designs rely on (verified by reading the files in this session):
- An idle agent is woken only if a question id appears that was not open when it went idle, or if there is news about its own filings; the comparison set `before` is taken once on entering the hold. — [starter-kit/agent.py, `Team.hook`](../../starter-kit/agent.py)
- The team finishes when every agent is idle and no extraction is pending. — [starter-kit/agent.py, `Team.hook`](../../starter-kit/agent.py)
- Every agent is shown all open questions; the prompt tells it to work on those its website can answer. — [starter-kit/agent.py, `briefing` and `INVESTIGATOR`](../../starter-kit/agent.py)
- A question is closed by id for good once any agent answers it (`answers[qid] = (status, note)`; `ask` skips ids in `answers`). — [starter-kit/casefile.py, `CaseFile.questions` and `CaseFile.answer`](../../starter-kit/casefile.py)
- The `material:<ref>` question embeds the current requirement values in its text and is emitted only when the requirement is complete and not waiting for a reserve; the matching itself is deterministic (`match_material`). — [starter-kit/casefile.py, `CaseFile.questions`](../../starter-kit/casefile.py)
- Extraction results and conflict notices are delivered only to the agent that filed the document (`news[agent]`); `_merge` returns the fields whose value was replaced; every extracted record is kept with its kind, source page and filing agent in `evidence`. — [starter-kit/casefile.py, `_extract`, `merge`, `_merge`](../../starter-kit/casefile.py)
- The agent loop keeps every past assistant reply (thought and actions) in the prompt and shortens only older user turns. — [starter-kit/worker.py, `Agent._messages`](../../starter-kit/worker.py)
- A coverage record (pages opened, text typed, lists followed) already gates "complete" and "absent", bounded to two refusals per question; it does not gate `done` and does not know which sections exist but were never opened. — [starter-kit/coverage.py, `Ledger.gate`](../../starter-kit/coverage.py)
- A repeated-action notice exists (same actions on the same page three times); there is no counter for "many different actions without any new fact". — [starter-kit/worker.py, `Agent.run`](../../starter-kit/worker.py)

External evidence each design leans on: prerequisite gating ([MetaGPT](https://arxiv.org/html/2308.00352v7), [LLMCompiler](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.04511)); volunteering after profiling ([Salemi et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.01285v2)); narrowing context ([LangChain](https://www.langchain.com/blog/benchmarking-multi-agent-architectures)); ledger and stall counter ([Magentic-One](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04468v1)); premise-linked retraction ([reason maintenance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_maintenance)); weak belief updating in models ([STALE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06527)); structural over prompt fixes ([MAST](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v3)); quiescence with in-flight work ([Dijkstra-Scholten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dijkstra%E2%80%93Scholten_algorithm)).

### Inferences

#### 7.0 Build order (about 3 to 3.5 hours in total)

| # | Change | Fixes | Files | Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Question objects with `basis`; answers and give-ups stamped with basis; level-triggered wake | missed wake-up; stale "absent"; part of stale rejection | casefile.py, agent.py | 40 min |
| 2 | CHANGED push to every agent that sees an affected question; drop old thoughts on change | stale rejection (46 turns) | casefile.py, worker.py | 30 min |
| 3 | Router learned from evidence provenance; source-scoped "not here"; lease and orphan widening | site-name routing; blind search (45 turns) | new router.py, agent.py | 60 min |
| 4 | Site card with grounded claims as routing prior and as section frontier for the gate | cold start of the router; one-folder search | agent.py, coverage.py | 45 min |
| 5 | TENTATIVE flag; refuse "absent" while tentative; superset wording | wasted and wrong work on unstable inputs | casefile.py | 20 min |
| 6 | Stall counter; completion test, last call and deadline reserve in `Team` | long unproductive stretches; early or late finish | worker.py, agent.py | 30 min |

Rules check for all six: code schedules, validates, notifies and retries; the model still chooses every navigation step, search term and document; nothing refers to a site name, layout or URL; question kinds come from the bid rules and the case-file schema, which do not change with the websites.

#### 7.1 Basis stamps and level-triggered wake (truth maintenance, minimal form)

```python
# casefile.py
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Question:
    qid: str
    text: str
    kinds: tuple[str, ...]   # evidence kinds that can answer it: knowledge of the rules, not of any website
    basis: str               # hash of the input VALUES the question was derived from
    tentative: bool = False  # see 7.3

def _basis(*values) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha1(repr(values).encode()).hexdigest()[:10]

# inside CaseFile.questions():
def ask(qid, text, kinds, basis_values=(), tentative=False):
    q = Question(qid, text, tuple(kinds), _basis(*basis_values), tentative)
    closed = self.answers.get(qid)                 # (status, note, basis, agent)
    if closed and closed[2] == q.basis:            # a conclusion holds only under the inputs it was made with
        return
    found.append(q)

# example: only the requirement values go into the basis, not the "on file for this group" list
ask(f"material:{ref}", text, kinds=("material",),
    basis_values=(facts.governing, need.catalogue_group, need.bore_mm, need.stroke_mm,
                  need.pressure_bar, need.mounting, need.certification))

# CaseFile.answer(): store the basis; a later change of the inputs reopens the question by itself
self.answers[question] = (status, note, current.basis, agent)
```

```python
# agent.py  Team: what each agent has given up on, by question VERSION
self.gave_up: dict[str, dict[str, str]] = {n: {} for n in names}      # agent -> {qid: basis}

def actionable(self, name) -> list[Question]:
    return [q for q in self.router.visible(name, self.case.questions())
            if self.gave_up[name].get(q.qid) != q.basis]

async def hold(why):
    for q in self.router.visible(name, self.case.questions()):
        self.gave_up[name][q.qid] = q.basis        # 'done' = I give up on these versions, nothing more
    self.idle.add(name)
    try:
        while not self.finished.is_set() and time.time() < self.deadline:
            await self.case.wait_change(self.case.version, 1.0)
            todo = self.actionable(name)           # LEVEL: anything visible to me in a version I have not given up
            if todo or self.case.news.get(name):
                return "The case file has news: " + ", ".join(
                    f"{q.qid} ({'changed' if q.qid in self.gave_up[name] else 'new'})" for q in todo)
            self.maybe_finish()                    # 7.5
        return None
    finally:
        self.idle.discard(name)
```
Effect: a corrected requirement changes the basis of `material:R`; the old "absent" no longer closes it; the idle agent is woken although the id is not new; a question newly routed to an agent by 7.2 wakes it for the same reason.

#### 7.2 Routing learned at run time: site card as prior, provenance as posterior, lease as safety net

```python
# router.py  (no site names anywhere; agents are opaque ids)
class Router:
    LEASE = 75.0   # seconds a READY question may stay without progress before more agents see it
    def __init__(self, agents):
        self.agents = list(agents)
        self.claim = defaultdict(dict)        # kind -> agent -> 0..1, from the agent's own site card (7.2b)
        self.hits = defaultdict(Counter)      # kind -> agent -> records extracted from that agent's filings
        self.not_here = defaultdict(set)      # (qid, basis) -> agents that searched and disclaimed
        self.level = Counter()                # (qid, basis) -> how often the question was widened
        self.since = {}                       # (qid, basis) -> time of first sight or last progress

    def score(self, kind, agent):
        if self.hits[kind][agent]:  return 1.0                      # evidence beats claims
        prior = self.claim[kind].get(agent)
        if prior is None:           return 0.5                      # no card yet: unknown, not zero
        return prior * (0.5 if any(self.hits[kind].values()) else 1.0)   # another site holds it; mine may hold some too

    def owners(self, q) -> set:
        key = (q.qid, q.basis)
        cand = {a: max(self.score(k, a) for k in q.kinds) for a in self.agents if a not in self.not_here[key]}
        if not cand:                                                # everybody disclaimed: orphan -> everyone, and flag it
            return set(self.agents)
        top, lvl = max(cand.values()), self.level[key]
        if top < 0.3 or lvl >= 2:                                   # nobody confident, or widened twice -> everyone left
            return set(cand)
        ranked = sorted(cand, key=cand.get, reverse=True)
        return {a for a in ranked if cand[a] >= 0.6 or cand[a] >= top - 0.1} | set(ranked[:1 + lvl])

    def visible(self, agent, questions):  return [q for q in questions if agent in self.owners(q)]

    def tick(self, questions, idle, now):                           # called once a second from Team
        for q in questions:
            if q.tentative: continue
            key = (q.qid, q.basis); self.since.setdefault(key, now)
            if self.owners(q) <= idle or now - self.since[key] > self.LEASE:
                self.level[key] += 1; self.since[key] = now         # widen; 7.1 then wakes the newly added agents
    def progress(self, kind, agent, now, questions):                # from CaseFile._extract after a successful merge
        self.hits[kind][agent] += 1
        for q in questions:
            if kind in q.kinds: self.since[(q.qid, q.basis)] = now
```

Semantics that make it degrade safely (invariants to unit-test):
1. Every open question is visible to at least one agent at all times (empty candidate set means everyone).
2. Unknown is 0.5, not 0: before cards and evidence exist, behaviour equals today's broadcast.
3. One extracted record of a kind from an agent's filing makes that agent an owner of that kind for the rest of the run, whatever the cards say.
4. "absent" from an agent means "not on my site": it is recorded in `not_here` for that question version and removes the question from that agent's view. The question closes as absent globally only when every agent with a positive score has disclaimed it, or when the disclaiming agent holds evidence of that kind (`hits > 0`) and passes the existing coverage gate.
5. A lease expiry or an all-owners-idle state widens visibility by one agent; the second widening shows the question to everyone who has not disclaimed it. Worst case under a wrong profile: one or two leases of delay.
6. Non-owners see one line instead of the question ("3 questions are with other agents"), so they neither work on them nor wonder whether the team has finished.

Briefing change (agent.py): replace the full list by `router.visible(name, case.questions())`, keep the case-file summary complete (shared context stays shared; only the to-do list is narrowed).

7.2b Site card (the prior, written by the model after its first look):

```text
Prompt addition (generic, no site knowledge):
  First look. Before you work on questions, take at most 4 turns to see what this website holds: its main
  sections, its search fields, the kinds of records. Then send
    {"do": "card", "holds": "<one sentence>",
     "sections": [{"name": "<label as shown>", "what": "<what is in it>"}],
     "can_answer": [{"kind": "<kind>", "confidence": 0.0-1.0, "seen": "<text on a page that makes you think so>"}]}
  Send the card again whenever you find a section that is not on it.
```
```python
async def card(action):                                   # agent.py, registered in `extra`
    seen_text = agent.pages_seen_text()                   # concatenation of observations so far (keep a rolling buffer)
    for c in action.get("can_answer", []):
        grounded = str(c.get("seen", "")).strip().casefold() in seen_text.casefold()
        conf = float(c.get("confidence", 0)) if grounded else min(float(c.get("confidence", 0)), 0.3)
        if c.get("kind") in SHAPES: router.claim[c["kind"]][name] = max(0.0, min(conf, 1.0))
    for kind in SHAPES: router.claim[kind].setdefault(name, 0.1)     # a card that omits a kind is a weak "no", never 0
    agent.card = action                                    # shown at the head of every later turn: YOUR WEBSITE (your notes)
    agent.coverage.sections = [s["name"] for s in action.get("sections", [])]
    case._bump(); return "card stored"
```
The card serves three purposes at once: routing prior (section 2), persistent memory of where things are on this site (the prompt today says the agent remembers only the page in front of it), and the section frontier for the coverage gate (7.5). If the model never sends a card, nothing breaks: every score stays 0.5 and the evidence posterior takes over.

Alternative when in-band cards prove unreliable with the fast model: one separate call per agent after its third turn (four calls in parallel, about 3 seconds), input = the agent's observed page titles and navigation labels plus the list of kinds with their one-line descriptions, output = the same `can_answer` list. This is contract-net bidding with a deterministic award; it is a model decision about its own source, not a hard-coded mapping.

#### 7.3 Dependency states: BLOCKED, TENTATIVE, READY

```python
# casefile.py: which open questions can still revise which fact groups (schema knowledge)
UPSTREAM = {"requirements": ("revision", "clarifications"),      # a revision switch or a Q&A amendment changes needs
            "material":     ("requirements", "clarifications", "reserve"),
            "data":         ("material",)}
FEEDS = {"requirements": ("revisions", "requirements", "clarifications"), "material": (...), ...}   # kinds whose pending extraction can change the inputs

def _tentative(self, family: str, open_ids: set[str]) -> bool:
    upstream_open = any(any(o == u or o.startswith(u + ":") for o in open_ids) for u in UPSTREAM.get(family, ()))
    feeding = any(self.pending_kind.get(k, 0) for k in FEEDS.get(family, ()))      # count pending per kind in file()/_extract()
    return upstream_open or feeding
```
- TENTATIVE questions are shown with a fixed suffix: "(inputs may still change: <which upstream question is open>. File every candidate of <stable attribute>; do not answer absent yet.)" and `CaseFile.answer` refuses "absent" for them.
- For `material:<ref>` the stable attribute is the catalogue group; filing the whole group makes a later correction of bore, stroke or pressure cost zero turns, because the deterministic matcher re-selects from what is on file.
- The router's lease clock does not run for tentative questions (7.2 `tick`).
- A blocked agent (nothing visible) does its bounded first look, sends its card, and is held. Add a hard cap: an agent with no visible question may take at most `SURVEY_TURNS` (for example 6) turns before `hold` is forced by the loop. This is the deterministic end of the 45-turn blind search.
- Risk: if an upstream question never closes (for example a Q&A list that is never marked complete), downstream questions stay tentative. Guard: tentativeness expires after a fixed share of the run (for example when 50% of the time is used) or when the upstream owner is idle and has given up on it.

#### 7.4 Change push and context hygiene

```python
# casefile.py: wrap every merge
def merge(self, kind, data):
    before = {q.qid: q for q in self.questions()}
    account = self._merge_records(kind, data)              # today's body of merge()
    after = {q.qid: q for q in self.questions()}
    for qid, q in after.items():
        old = before.get(qid)
        if old and old.basis != q.basis:
            line = (f"CHANGED [{qid}]: the facts this question rests on were corrected by a {kind} document. "
                    f"It now reads: {q.text[:300]} Anything you concluded about it before is void; "
                    f"candidates you set aside must be judged again.")
            for agent in self.router.owners(q) | self.router.owners(old):
                self.changes.setdefault(agent, []).append(line)
    return account
```
```python
# agent.py briefing(): changes go FIRST, before the case-file summary
changes = case.changes.pop(name, [])
text = ("CHANGES SINCE YOUR LAST TURN (read these first)\n" + "\n".join(f"- {c}" for c in changes) + "\n\n" if changes else "") + text
if changes: agent.forget_judgements()

# worker.py
def forget_judgements(self):
    """Keep what was done, drop what was concluded: older thoughts may state values that are no longer true."""
    for turn in self.turns[:-1]:
        reply = json.loads(turn["assistant"]); reply["thought"] = "(dropped: the case file changed since)"
        turn["assistant"] = json.dumps(reply, ensure_ascii=False)
        turn["user"] = turn["short"]                       # also drops old briefings that still show the old values
```
Why three mechanisms and not one: the basis stamp (7.1) retracts recorded conclusions and wakes sleepers; the CHANGED line makes the difference salient to an agent that is awake (STALE's finding that retrieval of the new value does not imply acting on it); dropping old thoughts removes the competing copies of the old value from the context. Optional stronger form, as in Magentic-One: clear `self.turns` completely on a change and rely on the briefing, the site card and the coverage record.

Related hardening (edge of scope): let authority decide which of two conflicting values is in use (current revision, later date, valid status) and use arrival order only as a tie-break, so that a superseded document filed late cannot overwrite a correct value.

#### 7.5 Stall counter, coverage of sections, and termination

```python
# worker.py: progress = this agent's filings changed the case file, or its coverage record grew
progress_mark = (case_hits_by(self.name), self.coverage.size())
...
if (case_hits_by(self.name), self.coverage.size()) == progress_mark: self.dry += 1
else: self.dry, progress_mark = 0, (case_hits_by(self.name), self.coverage.size())
if self.dry == STALL_TURNS:            # e.g. 7
    results.append("No new fact and no new page or search in 7 turns. Your open questions, as they read NOW: ... "
                   "Name a different place or search term, or finish with done.")
if self.dry >= 2 * STALL_TURNS:        # second stall: hold the agent, widen its questions to the other agents
    for q in team.router.visible(self.name, case.questions()): team.router.level[(q.qid, q.basis)] += 1
    finished = {"do": "done", "summary": "held after a stall"}
```
```python
# coverage.py: sections the agent itself listed on its card but never opened
def unopened(self) -> list[str]:
    opened = " ".join(self.views.values()).casefold() + " ".join(self.views).casefold()
    return [s for s in getattr(self, "sections", []) if s.casefold() not in opened]
# Ledger.gate(): before allowing "absent" (within the existing LIMIT of refusals):

```
The section names come from the model's own card, so nothing is tuned to a website; matching a label against page titles and addresses is a heuristic and stays bounded by the existing refusal limit.

```python
# agent.py  Team.maybe_finish(): called from every hold loop and once a second from a small supervisor task
def maybe_finish(self):
    now = time.time()
    if now >= self.deadline - RESERVE:                      # RESERVE = measured time to calculate, fill, sign, plus margin
        return self.finish("deadline reserve")
    if self.case.pending:                                   # work in transit: an extraction may still open a question
        self.settled = 0; return
    open_q = self.case.questions()
    if not open_q:                                          # nothing missing: stop now, do not wait for every 'done'
        return self.finish("complete")
    self.router.tick(open_q, self.idle, now)                # lease and orphan widening
    if self.idle != self.names:
        self.settled = 0; return
    pending_call = [(q, a) for q in open_q for a in self.names
                    if self.gave_up[a].get(q.qid) != q.basis and a not in self.router.not_here[(q.qid, q.basis)]]
    if pending_call and self.last_calls < MAX_LAST_CALLS:   # e.g. 2
        self.last_calls += 1
        for q, a in pending_call: self.router.level[(q.qid, q.basis)] = 2     # visible to all -> 7.1 wakes them
        return
    self.settled += 1
    if self.settled >= 2:                                   # two consecutive quiet checks: no race with a late merge
        self.finish("exhausted: " + ", ".join(q.qid for q in open_q))         # hand the open list to the bid step as flags
```
Decision table:

| State | Action |
|---|---|
| No open question, nothing pending | finish at once (complete) |
| Open questions, some agent working | keep going; lease clock runs |
| Open questions, all owners idle, another agent has not given up on this version | widen and wake (escalation) |
| Open questions, all agents idle and given up, nothing pending, last calls used | finish (exhausted), pass the open list on |
| Deadline minus reserve reached | finish whatever the state |

#### 7.6 Tests that can be written in the same sitting (no browser, fake case file)
- Change a requirement value after `material:R` was answered absent: the question is open again and the idle agent wakes within one tick.
- Give every agent a wrong card (the true holder claims 0.1): the question reaches the true holder after at most two leases; no question is ever invisible to all.
- All agents disclaim a question: it is shown to all once more and then reported as exhausted, never silently dropped.
- An extraction is pending while all agents are idle: the team does not finish.
- Delay injection: hold back one agent's extraction results by 60 to 120 seconds in a local run and compare the final case file with an undelayed run; they should be identical.

### Gaps
- None of the six changes has been run; turn counts, the lease length (75 s), the stall threshold (7 turns) and the survey budget (6 turns) are estimates to be tuned with the delay-injection test, not with knowledge of the public sites.
- Whether the fast non-thinking model writes usable site cards and calibrated confidences is unknown; the design therefore works without cards (everything starts at 0.5 and provenance takes over).
- The question-to-kinds table and the `UPSTREAM`/`FEEDS` tables must be filled from the actual rules in `casefile.py`; they encode the bid rules, not the websites, but they were only sketched here.
- If the final websites split one kind of record across two sites, the evidence posterior first favours the site found first; the 0.5 damping and the lease cover this, at the cost of one lease of delay. No measurement exists for how often this happens.
- The existing extraction kinds are named after document types of the public scenario (for example "mail"); whether those names fit other websites is outside this note but affects routing keys.

Research notes are written to:

D:\Personal_Projects\TUM_HackathonFinal\research_notes\Reliable multi site web agents\coordination_and_routing.md

(568 lines, 7 sections: the six key questions, each with Takeaway / Cited Findings / Inferences / Gaps, plus a seventh section with the concrete designs and pseudocode. Every finding carries an inline source and an evidence grade: [read], [abstract] or [search].)

## Main findings

**Architecture.** The described system is already a classic blackboard: case file = blackboard, site investigators = knowledge sources, `CaseFile.questions()` + `Team` = control shell. All four measured failures are control-shell defects, not a wrong architecture. Evidence points to keeping it and hardening the control code rather than adding an LLM orchestrator:
- Blackboard with volunteering beat a central master-slave controller by 13% to 57% relative on data discovery (Salemi et al., arXiv 2510.01285), at about 1.8x the cost.
- Magentic-One loses 31% on GAIA when its ledgers and loop detection are removed.
- LangChain's benchmark: a supervisor loses information by re-wording sub-agents; a single agent degrades sharply with two or more irrelevant domains in context (this matches the measured "own questions only" result).
- Anthropic lists tasks with many inter-agent dependencies as a poor fit for orchestrator-worker; its lead cannot steer running subagents.
- Scaling study (arXiv 2512.08296): multi-agent ranges from +80.8% on decomposable tasks to -70.0% on sequential ones.

**Routing.** The best-supported pattern is profile-then-volunteer. No paper measures missed questions or double work under a wrong profile, so safe degradation must be designed in.

**Stale beliefs.** Models often keep acting on an outdated premise even when the new value is retrievable (STALE benchmark, best model 55.2%). Published multi-agent systems mostly use supersession and re-reading; push and invalidation of derived conclusions are rare. Truth maintenance translates directly.

**MAST.** Step repetition 15.7%, unaware of termination 12.4%, premature termination 6.2%, ignored other agent's input 1.9%. Measured mitigations: prompt changes gain about 5 to 9 points; topology plus verification took ChatDev from 25.0 to 40.6. A secondary blog quotes different MAST percentages; the notes flag the conflict and use arXiv v3.

## Code observations that explain the bad runs (read in starter-kit, not run)

- `Team.hook` in `agent.py` wakes an idle agent only on a new question id or news about its own filings. A corrected `material:<ref>` keeps its id, so nobody is woken.
- `CaseFile.answers` closes a question by id for good, so an "absent" given under an old requirement value survives the correction.
- Conflict and extraction news go only to the filing agent.
- `Agent._messages` in `worker.py` keeps every old thought, so stale values stay in context.
- The coverage gate does not know which sections were never opened and does not gate `done`.

## Designs in section 7 (about 3 to 3.5 hours, all deterministic, no site names; untested)

## Main findings

**Architecture.** The described system is already a classic blackboard: case file = blackboard, site investigators = knowledge sources, `CaseFile.questions()` + `Team` = control shell. All four measured failures are control-shell defects, not a wrong architecture. Evidence points to keeping it and hardening the control code rather than adding an LLM orchestrator:
- Blackboard with volunteering beat a central master-slave controller by 13% to 57% relative on data discovery (Salemi et al., arXiv 2510.01285), at about 1.8x the cost.
- Magentic-One loses 31% on GAIA when its ledgers and loop detection are removed.
- LangChain's benchmark: a supervisor loses information by re-wording sub-agents; a single agent degrades sharply with two or more irrelevant domains in context (this matches the measured "own questions only" result).
- Anthropic lists tasks with many inter-agent dependencies as a poor fit for orchestrator-worker; its lead cannot steer running subagents.
- Scaling study (arXiv 2512.08296): multi-agent ranges from +80.8% on decomposable tasks to -70.0% on sequential ones.

**Routing.** The best-supported pattern is profile-then-volunteer. No paper measures missed questions or double work under a wrong profile, so safe degradation must be designed in.

**Stale beliefs.** Models often keep acting on an outdated premise even when the new value is retrievable (STALE benchmark, best model 55.2%). Published multi-agent systems mostly use supersession and re-reading; push and invalidation of derived conclusions are rare. Truth maintenance translates directly.

**MAST.** Step repetition 15.7%, unaware of termination 12.4%, premature termination 6.2%, ignored other agent's input 1.9%. Measured mitigations: prompt changes gain about 5 to 9 points; topology plus verification took ChatDev from 25.0 to 40.6. A secondary blog quotes different MAST percentages; the notes flag the conflict and use arXiv v3.

- Conflict and extraction news go only to the filing agent.
